conditions. To-day, to my amazement, the ' hon. member for Marquette stated that the farmers' co-operative companies could handle this matter just as well as any voluntary pool. The only redeeming feature to-day, apparently, is the compulsory feature, while in 1920 he argued very strongly against the compulsory feature, which he ranked with the Marxian idea of socialism. Evidently he has changed his views on this matter, and -today we find that the Minister of Agriculture and the leader of the Progressive party have arrived at the same conclusion with regard to the benefits to be derived from the continuance of this board.
We were also told by the Prime Minister this afternoon that a bill was now being prepared based on this report of the Agriculture Committee-this report which was arrived at in the manner I have indicated by a small representation of the committee after they had discussed the matter, according to the Minister of Agriculture himself, among themselves previously and arrived at an understanding as to what they would do. I would ask hon. gentlemen to explain to this House how it was they considered it advisable to change the report of the Agriculture Committee which had been adopted when there was a large representation present, and why the report of twenty-nine members of the committee who undertook to bring in this report upon which the bill is to be prepared, should be considered rather than the report of the seventy-eight who were present on May 23.
There are a number of other features in the report to which I should like to refer, but I shall not take up the time of the House. During the last election this question was a real live issue even outside the three western provinces. The leader of the Progressive party intimated that this question did not affect any other provinces, that the western provinces were the ones mostly concerned, but I have here a Canadian Press report of a meeting held at Walkerton, Ontario, on October 21,1921:
Government speakers, Mr. Crerar accused, were engaging in a "campaign of misrepresentation," and, in passing, Mr. Crerar took occasion to put a few questions in regard to the voluntary wheat pool formation of which, if it were returned to power, was indicated by Mr. Meighen in his opening speech at Portage la Prairie. If a wheat pool, Mr. Crerar queried, why should the government not furnish farm implemerts or market Ontario cheese? Why should the government not go into the business of marketing cattle? There should, Mr. Crerar urged, be a definite

pronouncement whether or not the business of marketing was to be a permanent feature of government policy.
So, Mr. Speaker, you will see that this question has invaded even the province of Ontario, and the leader of the Progressive party is the one who was responsible for that. I might say a good deal more about things which the hon. member for Marquette dealt with during the election in the province of Ontario, but I am not going to do so.
Now, unified control has not been resumed in the Old Land and wheat must follow the usual course in the matter of finding a market. It is argued that the appointment, of a wheat board would regulate the flow of wheat in Canada and stabilize prices in this country. Before the Agriculture Committee Mr. Wood was asked why not have the Wheat Board made permanent, and what do you suppose was his answer? I quote from the evidence :
Mr. McKay: If the Wheat Board is all that you claim it to be, why do you not ask for its re-establishment on a permanent basis?
Mr. Wood: Well, there are several reasons. There is a great deal of objection everywhere to that method of trading. I am not convinced that it would be a good thing to re-establish it on a permanent basis if there were no objections. Furthermore, a bad wheat board would be a bad institution. That is the reason we lay emphasis on the re-establishment of the old Wheat Board including largely the personnel of that board. That was an efficient body, and an efficient wheat board is a very satisfactory institution ; but I do not think tnat anything could be worse than a wheat board that was inefficient and mixed up with politics.
This was the opinion of the president of the Dominion Council of Agriculture with regard to the Wheat Board: There was a possibility, a great possibility of a wheat board getting the country into no end of a tangle, and consequently he is opposed to it being made permanent; but he had faith in the men who were on the old board and if they could be secured he thought we ought to try the system for another year.
Now, as to the compulsory feature of this agency, I do not like the word " compulsion " in any case. I believe that if we desired to promote business in this country we would have a much better result if we depended more on competition than on compulsion. I do not believe in the idea that some people have in this age, that it is the duty of the state to nurse people along, take care of them, think for them and do things for them that they should do for themselves. I do not believe

Wheat Board
that it is a sound doctrine to preach or to practice, and furthermore I do not think such to he in the interest of this country. If anything of value can be done to assist the grain growers in the West in regard to the marketing of their wheat I contend that it can only be done on a voluntary basis; and if you resort to compulsion I do not know where you are going to draw the line or where you are going to end up. Yet we are told in this debate that the compulsory features are the only advantages in the methods which can now be employed. I say, Mr. Speaker, that the fact that compulsion is necessary is the most objectionable feature of the proposals now before the House, and consequently in order to bring the matter to an issue in a concrete form-because I do not consider that the report which has been presented voices the opinion of the majority of the committee-I desire to move, seconded by Mr. Arthurs:
The said report be referred back to the select standing committee on Agriculture and Colonization with instructions to amend same to read as follows:
It is desirable in the national interests that the Government immediately create a national wheat marketing agency similar to the Canada Wheat Board of 1919, but on a voluntary basis fully in accordance with the powers of Parliament, for the marketing of the wheat crop of 1922, and that to this end federal legislation be introduced immediately, such legislation to provide further that the said board may, with the approval of the Governor in Council exercise such further powers or duties as may be competently conferred upon it by the legislature of any province.

speechtext:
I
had not intended until just within the last half hour to speak on this subject to-night. It is, however, true that I have been in->
tensely interested in it. I have worked as I could in the Agriculture Committee for the adoption of this action-to bring before the House the report which it is at present considering. The report was laid before the House some weeks ago and, speaking personally, I was quite content after the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had made his speech this afternoon and had told us that the policy of the Government was to let the matter rest there until the bill to be founded on the report had been submitted to us. I want to bear this tribute to the Prime Minister at least -that while we do not always see eye to eye with him or his Government, I think that in this measure, at least, he has redeemed his promises to the letter. The right hon. gentleman promised during the election campaign to submit this question
to a committee for investigation and, when that committee had agreed upon its report, to lay it before Parliament. In the exchange of political courtesies across the floor of the House I fear I can take little or no part. I will own myself vanquished before I start out, I am a novice at that kind of thing; and if hon. gentlemen derive any enlightenment from that sort of discussion, or if they think it advances their ideas to any extent whatever, they are entirely welcome to the belief.
Before proceeding further with what I intend to say I must refer to a few of the remarks that have been made during this debate. The last speaker (Mr. Sutherland), if I correctly understood him, wanted an explanation as to action taken at the last meeting of the Agriculture Committee. I may say that I interested myself in every meeting that was held, I was present at every one of the sittings from beginning to end, and I had no intimation with respect to that particular meeting other than the ordinary notification given in the case of all meetings. I believe that the meeting in question was called in the regular order, and if anything of an irregular character was done, or anything in a corner, I have no knowledge whatever of it. I knew, of course, of the suggested alterations in the report which 9 p.m. has been brought before the House and which went back to the committee. The suggestion has been made that the report was not acceptable to certain elements of the community. The only change in the wording of the resolution-though others may have been suggested-was by adding these words at the end of the second paragraph.
Except as they include the direct marketing of flour and other mill products.
There seems to be some difference of opinion as to how or why that was inserted. I think the discussion took place, as all hon. members discuss these things, perhaps not in a formal committee. If that is an offence, I am guilty. I have discussed the merits of this case, in different places around the House of Commons and on the streets, with private members from all groups in this House, and I did not hold myself guilty for that, because I was looking for light. Let me say candidly that I did not wish to see this amendment made. I wish to put myself on record to this effect, that the resolution as first introduced and passed at the first meeting more nearly met my views than anything else that could have been done.

Wheat Board

speechtext:
Absolutely. But when it went back to the committee, it was out of my hands and out of the hands of the sub-committee. I would have preferred it if the amendment had not been made; but I am going to tell the House why it was made. As to whether the procedure was in order or not in order, I am not an authority. The hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) will remember that, in the meeting of which he speaks, I took the same side as himself; I did not believe the procedure was in order; but I was no authority and I referred it to officers whom I do not like to name, but whom I regard as higher authorities than either the hon. member for Centre Vancouver or myself. That, however, has nothing to do with the matter. The fact is that the report was returned to the committee, and so far as I know the motion was rescinded in regular parliamentary order, and the amendment made.
Why was the amendment made? Accusation has been made in this debate that it was made at the instigation of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) or myself, or the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) or others, I know not whom, so far as I know, the alteration was made at the request of certain friends of the milling interests. They objected-and this was the ground of their argument-that it interfered with selling connections which they had already made in European and other foreign countries, or other places where they were marketing their products. That was the gist of their objection. I do not see yet how it should injure the farmers to allow the millers to retain those connections if they wish to retain them, provided that we have control of the wheat, and there is no question in the resolution that that should be yielded. It is a singular thing, however, that this was yielded at the request and so far as I know, only at

the request of the friends of the milling interests. When they made this request I said:	You are conducting an
honest and legitimate business in the country and I am perfectly willing that you or any one else shall be guarded as much as is possible. But a singular thing has happened; since this change has been made, representatives of the milling interests have come to me and said that they wished it had been left alone. I am not an authority on milling, and if those gentlemen who represent the milling interests cannot make up their minds just what it is they want, we are absolutely certain what we want embodied in the resolution and we have so passed it.
The hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) said something about compulsion. He did not like a thing of this sort being compulsory. There may be some merit in that contention; but I would refer him to the remarks made a few minutes ago by the Minister of Agriculture. It is compulsory, of course; but, although the term may seem anomalous, it is voluntary compulsion. The duty of this Parliament, as I see it, and the thing which we wish, is to pass an act giving to the Wheat Board all powers, compulsory or otherwise, which it is within the jurisdiction of this Parliament to grant; then if the people want that, they shall say to the local legislature whether this shall be compulsory or not. If they do not want it, it will go by the board, and nothing more will be heard of it.
I wish to refer to some remarks made by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen). I am not a lawyer; I believe he is, and as no doubt he is an able, clever lawyer, I shall not enter into a controversy with him. He raised certain questions and legal criticisms, and argued that the thing could not legally be enacted: that, if enacted, it could not function, and various other things. I will not contend with him in regard to these points; but knowing my lack of knowledge of this sort of thing, I had conferred with others. On two or three different occasions we have had the opinion of the law officers of the Crown on this subject, and I need not enumerate the occasions nor yet read the reports. I will, however, read an extract from the last report submitted after various consultations with the Deputy Minister of Justice and his written opinion on certain features of the matter, supported by conclusions of the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) and the Solicitor General (Mr. McKenzie) in some respects. This

Wheat Board
is the conclusion arrived at, and so far as I know, it stands as the opinion of those gentlemen to-day.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman has misunderstood my argument. I do not see legal objections at all. There is no doubt, within the two jurisdictions, the provincial legislature and the federal Parliament, everything can be done that the people of Canada or of those provinces wish. The difficulties I see are not legal at all; they are difficulties in practical operation where certain compulsory powers are conferred in one province that do not exist in the province immediately beside it.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
I am glad to have the correction. I did not so understand my right hon. friend; nevertheless, I should like, now that I am on the subject, to give to the House the decision arrived at by the sub-committee, based on the report from the law officers of the Crown. It is very brief:
In conclusion, the deputy minister expressed the view that by legislation passed partly by the Dominion and partly by the provinces, it was legally possible to control:
(a)	The acquisition of all wheat raised in any provinces passing such legislation;
(b)	The storing of the wheat so acquired in country elevators;
(c)	The storing of such wheat In terminal elevators even though those elevators be situated in provinces other than those passing laws for the compulsory acquisition of wheat.
(d)	All export and import trade in wheat and wheat products.
There is only one other question that was asked of the law officers of the Crown, and it is in reference to terminal facilities. While I have the report open at the page, I will also read that short extract for the benefit of the House, because terminal facilities are essential to the carrying on of this business. This is an extract from the report of the sub-committee:
That in conference concerning this question we intimated that the "use" referred to in the first line of this question.-
That is in reference to the elevators.
-was to be interpreted as exclusive use. The view verbally expressed to us by the deputy minister was that the use of elevators owned by the Dominion could be exercised in any manner by the Dominion government; that as to privately owned elevators such could be declared works for the general advantage of Canada, and when so declared would fall under federal jurisdiction.
I had other references to support my contention. Seeing that the leader of the Opposition has concurred in that as well, it is no longer a matter of contention, and
I will not repeat them. We can see that there is, within the various parliaments, provincial and federal, the power to enact this legislation and, in my opinion, all the things we asked for as regards the Wheat Board can be granted to us in that way.
I will now proceed to deal with a few thoughts and notes which I had prepared on this subject, things which I have considered in connection with it. It may seem a political matter, but I want to refer first to the attitude of the three parties within this House on the question now under consideration. I believe that all three have consistently lived up to their platform in this respect. I have no criticism to oifer and no political slams to make at any one. The Progressives have stood from the beginning for a compulsory wheat board, in other words, for the re-establishment of the board as it was in 1919. I regret that the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) has not taken a better stand than he has.
I did not expect that at this stage he would have been so emphatically in favour of a voluntary system. While I believe he was perfectly sincere in advocating it, I cannot conceive how an hon. gentleman of his intelligence, and men like those around him, can longer hold the view they express in spite of the decision rendered in the recent election. I know of no propaganda-I will not say that it was purely for political purposes, because I believe he was sincere in it-that ever fell so flat and struck so unresponsive a chord as did that proposition in western Canada. And there was a reason for it. Men who had made a lifelong study of this thing, having worked on it for years and made it their sole business, from the middle of July, 1920, for eighteen months, concentrated their efforts towards a solution of the problem, and they came to the conclusion that the system advocated by my right hon. friend was not practical. As I proceed I shall deal to some extent with the voluntary pool system and state why, in my opinion, it is not practical. The matter was dealt with by the leader of this party (Mr. Crerar) this afternoon. The Liberal party's policy on the question I described at the outset, and they too have been consistent. I do not think that they have gone as far as they should. They have a responsibility as a government to solve this problem and to solve it right, in view of the circumstances in which we are placed.
Before I go further I shall anticipate some of the objections that may be offered, one of which was mentioned this evening.
Wheat Board

Some hon. member, I do not know just who, said that while this board was being asked for as a temporary measure, possibly, with mental reservations, it might be made permanent. Well, if by permanency hon. gentlemen mean a permanent, satisfactory solution of the wheat marketing problem, i I hope it will be permanent. But I have yet to hear any one advocating that this measure with regard to the compulsory wheat board should be made permanent. I do not believe that any one seriously thinks so. In case some hon. gentlemen may think that this is a new opinion on my part, I may say that at the very first meeting in the recent campaign, when I addressed my own nominating convention, I was asked the question whether I would favour a compulsory wheat board, and I replied, for this year only until readjustment is achieved, but not as a permanent policy, because I believed in the co-operative system of a wheat marketing agency operated and controlled by the producers of wheat. I still stand by that opinion, and I think that the ultimate solution will have to be found there. From the very nature of the product, which is so widespread and of such magnitude, it is impossible for us at the present time, facing the critical situation in which we are placed, to solve the problem without assistance, and we have come to the federal Parliament to ask their aid. And it is my hope and belief that out of this measure, if it is made effective this year, will be organized that voluntary co-operative system which we hold as our ideal.
It has been stated, not in this debate, but frequently in the debate that was concluded last night, and the matter has been made the subject of some gibes at our expense, that we are asking for protection. Well, we are asking for protection, but it is the sort of protection I believe in. I believe in police protection. But the protection, as I understand it, which hon. gentlemen to my right have been advocating during the last few weeks is a form of protection that I cannot tolerate. It is a restriction, misnamed protection, that is imposed on others; some one else has to pay for the protection that is afforded. But I have yet to hear any one claim or prove that anybody will pay for this protection. Nor do I ask for our own industry protection. I believe also in protecting the public from the depredations of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and of the Canadian manufacturers. I believe in protecting the wheat producers from ex-

ploitation at the hands of the grain merchants. But if it were proposed that some one else should be made to suffer in consequence I would not advocate such protection. Nor do I ask for our own industry, any form of protection that I am not willing to grant to others.
It has also been stated, and this can ibe proved, that we are creating a monopoly. Well, I ask you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. gentlemen in this Chamber, to consider this fact. The figures furnished me by the Bureau of Statistics shows that the Canadian production of wheat is about 300,000,000 bushels per anurn. Now, can anyone conceive, even by the wildest stretch of imagination, how the Canadian wheat producers, with 300,000,000 bushels of wheat, can have a monopoly in the world market where the annual production is over 3,000,000,000 bushels? Our product is sold in the markets of the world in open competition with wheat from all parts of the globe.
This House, I think, is weary of the hard luck tale from the western prairies; it is perhaps tired of the story of poverty and hardship. Having pioneered in the western country twenty-five or thirty years ago, I should not care, with the personal recollection of those hardships, to rehearse the story now. I want to deal briefly with the matter, however, from another angle; I want to take it up from the business point of view, and I hope it will appeal to hon. gentlemen. It is granted, readily, I think, that all, or at least most businesses were unprofitable during the past year; and certainly that is true in regard to the agricultural industry of the West, particularly in the growing of wheat, which has not been done at a profit. But that condition is not confined to last year, and I will submit a few brief statements to show you the cost of producing wheat. Let me quote from the evidence of the Hon. C. M. Hamilton, Minister of Agriculture in the province of Saskatchewan. He is a man who is in a position to know, and he found that on the average farm in that province the total expenditures were $4,107.10 while the revenue amounted to $2,221.40, leaving an annual deficit of $1,885.70. Do hon. gentlemen think that it is in the national interest that such a condition should longer prevail? I want to quote from another authority, 'Superintendent McKillican of the Brandon Experimental Farm. His annual report shows that the cost of producing wheat on a selected pa tch

Wheat Board
of land on the experimental farm is $1.30 per bushel, making no allowance whatever for freight to take it to the markets of the world. If you add freight you will find that the cost is something like $1.45 a bushel, while we know that the average price of wheat during the past year has been much below that figure.

speechtext:
Mr. Hamilton's
evidence was with regard to the average farm of 320 acres. I notice that the returns he gives are confined entirely to wheat and oats. Surely those figures do not represent the total returns from the whole farm.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Hamil ton was speaking of a grain farm, and if my hon. friend knows Saskatchewan as I know it, he will agree that in the vast majority of cases the growing of grain is the only occupation that can be carried on satisfactorily. There are sections where mixed farming can be carried on, but even that is done at an equally great loss.
I want to make one other reference, and it should appeal to business men. Recently in conversation with an hon. member from the Maritime provinces he gave me a secondhand scolding because certain municipalities in western Canada had defaulted on their bonds, and he stated the East had supplied the money for those bonds. That condition is only a reflection of the difficulties and handicaps under which our greatest commodity is produced. Let me give another conversation-this time with a banker in Moosejaw about a year ago. He told me that his headquarters had been protesting against his having valued farms in that district too high for credit purposes. I think he had, for although they were selling there at from $100 to $125 an acre, he had valued them at $100 an acre. I was able to show him a farm which had actually paid a 5 per cent dividend on a $100 per acre valuation, and he felt elated. But last spring in a conversation with him he told me that he had been instructed to cut the valuation of farm lands absolutely in two, and that a $100 an acre farm for credit purposes is now worth only $50 an acre.
Various factors might help the situation, and the wheat board is one. I do not wish to introduce anything irrelevant to this discussion, but I might refer to two subjects which we have heard something about and which will come before us again. Dealing first with freight rates, I find that the average farmer in the province of
Saskatchewan had to pay $206.61 more for freight on grain alone in 1922 than in 1917, or if you take the peak, $270.39. The other item is tariff regulations. When the tariff commission was wandering through western Canada a year or two ago I made a very careful statement covering eight years close bookkeeping on a farm, and I found that that farm was paying $300 per year more than it should pay on account of the customs tariff.
Now I come more particularly to the wheat board. There are several classes of the community who it is said, would be vitally affected if this wheat board is brought into operation. The first class is the consumers, and in this connection I am going to quote from the evidence given before the Agriculture Committee. Dr. Magill, Secretary of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, in answer to the question, "Was the consumer sacrificed?" said:
Well, there is no consumer in the world that I know of who was better treated-none, in my judgment, better treated, so far as most of our consumers are concerned. There was one class of them not protected, but that was not the fault of the Wheat Board.
And he goes on to say that there were certain people living in cities who bought their bread ready made. I will also quote from the evidence of Mr. Stewart, chairman of the old wheat board, who of all others should know the effect that the wheat board of 1919 had on the consuming public. The hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) asked:
Q. The statement has been .made that due to the action of the Wheat Board the price of flour was enhanced to the Canadian consumer, and that if the Wheat Board were reconstituted now it would mean an advance in the price of flour to the consumer in Canada?- A. As a matter of fact, the Canadian Wheat Board have never stated it before, but the price at which the Canadian consumer got his flour was relatively less than that received for the wheat which was exported as raw material; so that the Canadian consumer paid less than the world's price.
Another class that might be affected by the creation of this wheat board is the millers. I have already dealt with them. It has been amply proved in the evidence before the Agricultural Committee that the big millers are well able to take care of themselves, as is apparent in the facts and figures of the dividends they have paid.
As to the dealers, we have (been told that it would practically put them out of business. Let us hear what the Secretary of the Grain Exchange, Dr. Magill, has to say on that point:
Wheat Board

We appreciate very deeply the fact that the representations of the farmers before this committee took a very high level. The farmers argued their case on what they believed to be genuine economic grounds and we desire to do the same. The next remark I wish to make is this: judging from some reports one would imagine that the Winnipeg grain trade and the Wheat Board, the old Wheat Boarc,, stood in the relation of mortal enemies. Now, what were the facts? When the Wheat Board got together under the Defence of the Realm Act what did they do? They negatiated with the Winnipeg grain trade, and the negotiation resulted in the employment by the Canada Wheat Board of nearly the whole of the trade. The Wheat Board when it met had no elevators, and the Government had no elevators to give it. They had no elevator managers or staff. The Wheat Board called in and employed the companies that manager what the farmer members themselves have described before this committee as the splendid, the almost unsurpassed machinery for the handling of grain that we possess in Canada. The Wheat Board called in the grain trade. The Wheat Board used the elevators. The Wheat Board used the managers. The Wheat Board used the staffs and the elevators from the Atlantic to the Pacifl.2. The Wheat Board employed the lake shippers for the loading of boats. They employed the clearing houses. They employed the brokers. They employed the commission men, and they employed the freight shippers and the exporters to take the grain at Fort William and place it at the seaboard for them. The Wheat Board employed, I suppose, 75 per cent or perhaps 80 per cent of the existing grain trade at Winnipeg. Not only did they employ them; they paid them. They paid them a fair and reasonable return for their services, and if we at the present time object to the recreation of the Wheat Board, it is not because of any specific deal; it is not because they did not treat us fairly and reasonably; it is not because we have any belief that they failed in their services-they rendered splendid service,-I am speaking of the Wheat Board-not merely to the producers of this Dominion, but to the whole of this Dominion. It is not for such reasons as that that we appear here to-day to make a case on the other side.
I have never been able to discover what case they did make out, but on the authority of the secretary of the Grain Exchange they were willing to offer their services, and they were employed. It has been said that the operation of a wheat board would have some effect on the transportation companies. Before the Agriculture Committee I made this statement, and I make it again. It was given to me by an official of one of our railways. He said that if they were permitted to handle the wheat crop of western Canada, spreading it out over nine months, instead of rushing it on in the early part of the season, it would save to that company alone 22,000 cars. Surely that is a consideration worth while.
For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I believe that no section of the community would be injuriously affected by the reinstatement

of the Canadian Wheat Board, but that on the contrary many of those who produce wheat would be saved from absolute destruction. Some one said to-night that if we are so unanimous in favour of a voluntary pool, why, we could have the whole thing anyway. Well, this may sound somewhat harsh, but I know there are hundreds and thousand's of farmers in western Canada whose creditors would not allow them to take advantage of a voluntary pool. The statement which I am going to make may sound like a hard one, but it has been given to me in good faith and I believe it to be true. There are farmers in western Canada to-day to whom a big crop this year would be a positive disaster. That may seem unbelievable, but here is the reason: there are farmers in that country who are so much in debt owing to lack of crops and depreciated values during the past few years that one good crop would not relieve them. If they have a good crop their creditors would come after them, and even if 90 per cent of their creditors would wish to be lenient and the rest did not, the others would be forced in self-defence to come in and make their claim, and that farmer would be sold out.
I will not deal further with the voluntary pool. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) dealt with it this afternoon. If we want a voluntary pool, any few of us can get together for that purpose, if we can afford to do so; we do not require legislation for that. But it would not relieve the situation; far from doing so, it would be a positive menace to the farmers of western Canada.
Reference has been made, I believe by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), to the question of financial responsibility. In my opinion there is only one logical place to put the financial responsibility, the financial risk, in this connection, and that is right on the people who produce the wheat. I do not know of a single farmer who wants to shirk in any degree his share of responsibility for any loss which may be incurred. But is a loss possible? As a result of the operations in 1919-and that is a pretty good criterion-so far from having a loss the board actually turned back to the government $560,000 and had over $200,000 in their hands besides in the way of participation certificates. It might be all right to put the financial responsibility on the provinces, to let them take care of any deficits that might occur and, of course,

Wheat Board
share also in any surpluses. We have no objection to that, provided the control of the board is safeguarded-that there is to be no divided control. The experience of 1919 taught us one thing more than anything else, namely, that it is essential that there be unified or, practically, one-man control of this institution if it is to be successful. We were satisfied with the 1919 board, Mr. Speaker, and we ask the Government to come as near to it as they possibly can. Then, if the provinces see fit to come in and take advantage of it, that is all we can ask.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish unduly to delay the House at this late hour in the discussion of this report. But I have spent a great deal of time on this question and have given it a good deal of study, and after listening to the evidence I have come to the conclusion, which has beeen fortified and deepened by the study I have since made of the subject, that the proposed wheat board, whether it gets its power entirely from this jurisdiction or partly from this and partly from another jurisdiction, is an unwise proposal, and I am going to ask the indulgence of hon. members while I place before them the reasons why I will vote against the adoption of this report. I will not vote in favour of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), because he wishes to put the whole grain trade of this country in the hands of a couple of men, in the hands of a board, and I am opposed to that as well. Let me as briefly and as succinctly as I can give to hon. members the reasons which have led me to this conclusion.
Now what is the proposal? It is that the old Canada Wheat Board of 1919 be reconstituted; that part of its powers be drawn from this House and part from the legislatures of any of the provinces-which cannot be other than the prairie provinces -that desire to invest it with such authority. Now, what were these powers? Let us examine them for a moment. They had the right-I will not say, to purchase the wheat, but to expropriate it without the consent of the owner. They had the power to order any person holding wheat stored in any elevator or warehouse or railway cars or Canadian boats to sell and dispose of the same to any purchaser named by the board on such terms as the board might direct; and it was provided that any such order of the board should pass to the purchaser the title in the wheat mentioned in any such order. They had the right to require that any wheat sold or purchased in Canada should be delivered to the board or to its order in accordance with such regulations as the board might from time to time make. I know of no other occasion on which such power has been conferred on any one person or group of persons since Pharoah gave Joseph the right to gather up all the corn in Egypt and make the greatest corner in history. But not only is that the fact; they were to have the right to prohibit the export out of or importation into Canada of any wheat or wheat products otherwise than in accordance with the regulations and orders of the board.

speechtext:
May I ask
the hon. gentleman a question? Did not Joseph save Egypt under those circumstances?

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
Yes, Joseph saved Egypt, but at the cost of bringing all the people into bondage. If my hon. friend wants that, perhaps he will vote for the reconstitution of the Wheat Board. Now, the power to prohibit importation into or export from a country is a power which this board will have to derive from this House; it can come only from this jurisdiction. By an Order in Council of the 31st of July the board had the right, notwithstanding anything in the Railway Act, notwithstanding anything in the Grain Act, to compel railway companies to provide cars for transportation; and finally, so that nothing should be wanting in the powers which were given, they had the right to legislate criminally and to create offences dealing with any infraction of the regulations of the board. The fact that any persons in this country should at this time seriously propose the reconstitution of a wheat board of this sort is a sad reflection on the value placed on liberty for its own sake, and also a very high compliment to the wisdom and the moderation of the gentlemen who in the past had such great powers vested in them. They must have used those powers with care, wisdom and moderation.
Now, I might anticipate an objection which will be raised. Gentlemen who advocate this wheat board will say: "You are borrowing trouble; we are not asking from this House the right to expropriate; we will get that from one of the prairie provinces." Well, to my mind the man who boldly does a thing that is wrong is
Wheat Board

to be preferred to the man, who, knowing a thing is wrong, steps aside to let another man do it. As a matter of fact, under our criminal law an accessory before the fact is held to be just as guilty as the man who himself commits the crime. It reminds me of the tales we have heard of the past when white civilized races were fighting each other on this continent in the eighteenth century: one would charge against the other that they had abandoned prisoners to their Indian allies to deal with them as they wished. I do not propose, if by my feeble voice I can prevent it that principles I have cherished for years shall be bound to the stake and burnt up by a wheat board.
Now let me say as succinctly as I can, and I trust with perfect accuracy, and I will invite members opposite to correct me if I am not perfectly accurate, what I understand to be the case for the wheat board. As I understand it, the advocates for the wheat board say this: They say that they harvest their crops in the latter part of August and perhaps all through September; that they are obliged through the economic pressure of their creditors to bring that crop to market in the months of September, October, November and December, when they really should be doing their fall ploughing, and when the cost of threshing is high; that by this fact they are obliged to throw such an amount of wheat upon the market that it is glutted and the price pushed down; and that after they have disposed of their wheat the price rises. That, I understand, is the statement of the case made by the advocates of the Wheat Board.
Now my contention is, and I propose to submit to the House, and to you, Mr. Speaker, figures to prove it, that such is not the case; that if you take one special year you may find that the price is lower in the autumn months than in the months of March, April and May succeeding, but that if you take any considerable number of years and compare the prices realized in the fall months of the crop year with the prices paid in the spring months of the crop year, you will find precisely the reverse. I state that the figures will show that taking one year with another it is good business for the farmer to sell his wheat in the fall months. I know I have to prove this to many members of the House who entertain a different notion, and whose business should enable them to have much more accurate information 
than I have, but I have endeavoured to examine the figures with care and to collate them in such a way that I believe I can show to those who will give ear to me that I am right-
There is no use, Mr. Speaker, taking the few past years as the years on which to base your argument, because the few last years have either been war years or years immediately succeeding the war, when the ordinary markets of the world were disturbed. The proposal that I make, Mr. Speaker, is that in fairness to our argument we take the six crop years which ended on the 31st of August, 1914-the crop years 1908-1909, 1909-1910, 1910-1911, 1911-1912, 1912-1913 and 1913-1914. I shall have to cite a good many figures, but I hope the House will bear with me. I have made two comparisons. First I have compared the highest figure in the month of September with the highest figure in the month of March.

speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman think it is quite fair to make that comparison? Because the basis of our desire to have a wheat board is the fact that we have not yet reached normal marketing conditions and that we are still suffering from the after effects of the war? Therefore, it should be the later years, and not the years before the war, that should be taken into account.

When the board was formed in 1919, there was collective buying in Europe, and therefore good grounds for urging collective selling in Canada. When the suggestion was made, I think, in the session of 1920, that we should have a reconstitution of the Wheat Board it was held then that as there was decontrol to a large extent in Europe there should be de-control in Canada, and my belief is that we are getting back to normal. It is true that getting back to normal has been largely at the expense of the primary producer, but as there is no control in Europe now, practically speaking, as there is no collective buying in Europe, I cannot see any reason for collective selling on this side of the Atlantic, and that being the case I think it is fair to take the normal years prior to the war rather than the abnormal years during or since the war. That is my contention. What do the six normal years prove? I do not know whether I need to go over these figures. I shall be glad to do so if hon. members will not be wearied

Wheat Board
with them, but let me perhaps first take the results of my investigation, and then if anyone doubts the correctness of those results I shall be glad to give the figures themselves.
I have taken the highest figure in September of 1908 and compared it with the highest figure in March, 1909, compared the highest figure in October, 1908, with the highest figure in April, 1909, and the highest figure in November, 1908, with the highest figure in May, 1909, and I do find in connection with that crop year that it would have paid farmers, though not to any great extent, to have held on to their wheat until the spring.

speechtext: If it is the year 1908 my hon. friend is taking, the price goes up from $1 to $1.35 in June.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext: I say that that is the one striking year of these six years when it would have paid the wheat grower to have hung on.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
I think I can deal with that afterwards. I propose, first of all, to give these figures, and then treat them in relation to the visible supply, which I think will answer to a certain extent, at least, the desires of my hon. friend who has just put the question. With his permission, let me proceed along the line I have indicated.
I have also taken for this crop year the average price for the month. I think perhaps it makes a better comparison to take the average price during the month of September and compare it with the average price for March, and compare October with April, and November with May. In order to make the comparison equal, I have added 9 cents a bushel for the six months, representing li cents a bushel per month, so that the price in September of $1 would be just as good to the grain grower as the price of $1.09 in March. I think that is fair. On that basis of comparison during 1908-1909, if the grain grower had held on to his grain until March instead of selling it in September, he would have made 2.7 cents a bushel; if he had held on until April instead of selling in October, he would have made 12.5 cents a bushel, and if he had held on until May instead of selling in December, he would have made 14 cents
a bushel. If you took that year by itself, I would say that the protagonists of the Wheat Board had gone a long way to prove their case, but that would be merely another case of the fallacy of arguing from the particular to the general.
If we take the other five years we will find a very different result. I would imagine from the expression on the faces of hon. gentlemen opposite that they believe that the average price gives a truer comparison than the highest point in the months for which I am making my comparison. Therefore to facilitate my argument and save time I will deal with the average prices merely, though I have worked the matter out by comparing highest prices with highest prices as well as average prices. Now, if we take the year 1909-10 we will find that if the grain-grower sold in September rather than holding on till March he would have made 2.2 cents more per bushel; that if he had sold in October rather than holding on till April he would have made 4.3 cents per bushel; that if he had sold in November rather than holding on till May he would have made 11.9 cents per bushel. That year is a strong piece of evidence that it does not pay the farmer-it certainly did not pay the farmer in that year-to hold his wheat, but rather to sell in the autumn months. Let me take the next year, 1910-11. If the grain-grower had sold in September rather than holding on till March in that year he would have made 20.9 cents per bushel; if he had sold in October instead of holding on till April he would have made 14.5 cents per bushel; and if he had sold in November rather than holding on till May he would have made 6 cents per bushel. That certainly is even a stronger year for my contention that the autumn months are the months in which it is wise for the agriculturist to sell his wheat. Now let us take 1911-12. We find that the grain-grower who sold in September rather than holding on till March made 11 cents per bushel; that he who sold in October rather than holding on till April made 6.4 cents per bushel, and that he who sold in November rather than holding on till May made 3.5 cents per bushel; another year in which it was more advisable for the farmers to sell in the autumn months. Then if we take 1912-13 we find that the grain-grower who sold in September rather than holding on till March made 19 cents per bushel; that he who sold in October rather than holding on till April made 8.7 cents; that
Wheat Board

he who sold in November rather than holding on till May lost 1.2 cents per bushel. Then if we take the next year, 1913-14, we find that the grain-grower who sold in September rather than holding till March made 5 cents per bushel; that he who sold in October rather than holding till April lost .6 cents per bushel; and that he who sold in November rather than holding till May lost 1.5 cents per bushel. I say, Mr. Speaker, that if these figures are correct there is no reasonable deduction to be drawn from them other than the fact that the three autumn months which I have compared are better marketing months than the three spring months I have mentioned.
I now come to deal with the point raised by my hon. friend who asked me the question as to quantity. In the committee, Mr. Speaker, I produced certain figures showing the average yearly price in Winnipeg, and the average yearly price in London for these six years on which I base my argument. I found, on these figures prepared for me by the Bureau of Statistics, that, taking one year with another, the carrying charges and profits made on the wheat, established on the difference between Winnipeg and London prices, amounted to 8J cents per bushel over the six years. One of the hon. members challenged the soundness of my conclusion. His statement was that these average prices mean very little because they are often obliged in a month to sell at the Lower prices, and therefore the average price does not give a true reflection of the real situation. In an endeavour to see whether there was anything in this contention I obtained the figures for the visible supply from week to week during these six years. Now I think hon. members will agree with me in my argument, that if it is the placing of Canadian wheat in large quantities on the Canadian market which forces prices down, then when there is least Canadian wheat in sight the prices should go up. That would be a fair deduction to draw. If it is the Canadian wheat which establishes the price we would expect to find, therefore, that where the visible supply increased, prices tended to fall; that where the visible supply decreased, prices tended to rise. That is not shown to be true by an examination of the figures. There is no apparent direct and constant reflection in the price of wheat of the smallness or the largeness of the visible supply. I had prepared a statement taking 296 weeks-that would 
be the six years, 296 weeks, or at least if that is not quite the six years it would be the weeks in which reports of the visible supply are made. There were 296 occasions on which visible supply was compared with decrease or increase in price, and what did I find? Increase in visible supply was accompanied not by decrease in price, as we would expect, but by increase in price 67 times; that increase in supply was accompanied by what we would expect-namely decrease in price- only 61 times; and that increase in visible supply on 6 occasions made no difference in the price at all. Now let us look at what happened in relation to decrease in visible supply. Decrease in visible supply was accompanied by an increase in price-and that is what we would expect-92 times; by a decrease in price, which we would not expect, 66 times; and by no change in price at all 4 times, making in all 162 times. That covers the whole 296 comparisons of visible supply with increase or decrease in price; and my argument is that it does show that there is no constant or necessary relation between the increase or decrease of visible supply and the price.
The conclusion that I am driven to is that we must seek other factors in the situation to explain the varia-10 p.m. tions of price in wheat in Canada, because the decrease or increase of visible supply will not explain the situation. Do the figures on other grain exchanges bear out the contention of hon. gentlemen opposite that there is a glut in the market in the fall months? I have discovered; in fact, it was placed before the Agriculture Committee that, taking the years 1895 to 1914, the supply of No. 1 Northern wheat in Minneapolis averaged in October for those nineteen years 85.3 cents per bushel while the average price in April was 88.3 cents per bushel. If we take the cost of carrying in Minneapolis at the same figure as in Winnipeg,-and I do not think that would be unfair-the grain grower who sold his wheat in October was six cents better off than the man who held his wheat until April; that is, as a general thing, taking into consideration the whole nineteen years. If we take the Chicago grain market, and if we take a period of fifty years,-and that should be a long enough period to give us reliable figures-if the arguments of the advocates of the Wheat Board are right, we should find that in the large majority of the years contained within those fifty years the lowest price would occur in the three au-

Wheat Board
tumn months, because that is when the grain comes upon the market. But what do we find? We find that the highest point on cash wheat was reached four times in September and five times in December; that is to say, nine times in fifty years this has happened. When was the lowest price found? We would expect to find the lowest price generally in those four months but it happened four times in September and five times in December, not the lowest price, but the highest price was reached. I thank hon. gentlemen for having paid such attention to those dry figures and I will now pass to another consideration of the matter.
In the Agriculture Committee, I asked Mr. Riddell who appeared as a witness before that committee, this question. I said: "You were fortunate m your administration of the Wheat Board of 1919. You were able to realise handsome figures for the wheat which passed through your hands and the names of Stewart and Riddell are blessed throughout western Canada. What would have happened if the market had gone the other way?" And Mr. Riddell answered, with perfect frankness and western freshness, that they would have been damned just as much as they had been blessed. The western folk who wish to have the Wheat Board are very anxious that it should be a Stewart and Riddell Wheat Board. They want Mr. Riddell; they want Mr. Stewart, and they do not seem to have any great confidence in other people. That, of course, is a sign of weakness in itself, because any legislation which must depend on the personality of two persons who are open to the vicissitudes of humanity is dangerous legislation. They might both be carried off by an epidemic; they might both be sick or be obliged to leave the country for one reason or another. But the strange feature of the matter is that neither Mr. Riddell nor Mr. Stewart are really enthusiastic protagonists of the Wheat Board. Mr. Stewart hails from Scotland. Not only has he the ability of mind which appertains to the Scottish race, but he is also endowed with no small degree of that nation's caution and prudence. He was asked the question in plain language: Are you in favour of a Wheat Board? And, if you will turn to page 273 of the evidence, you will see his answer which reads:
Q. Mr. Stewart of Humboldt read from the evidence of Dr. Magill in which he maintained that the consumer was well treated under the operations of the old Wheat Board under the conditions that existed at that time. Do you consider that the consumer would be well treated under present conditions if a compulsory Wheat Board were put into operation, and would it reflect to the general benefit of the Dominion of Canada?-A. If I expressed an opinion on that would it not really amount to contempt of court? This committee must determine that. I can only talk from practical experience, and tell you exactly what happened during the regime of the old Wheat Board.
Q. I do not think it involves contempt of court. We call witnesses to obtain their opinion, and there are in this committee a great many men who are very anxious to do the .best thing with regard to the question of a Wheat Board.
I think we have the right to ask your opinion, because you were a member of tne old Wheat Board?-A. Well, the Wheat Board as an economic proposition is a good one: but, on the other hand, the measure of public opinion which would be in favour of such a project would be a matter that would have to be taken into consideration by this committee.
Answers largely couched in the terms of the subjunctive mood. Then we have another question:
It is quite evident that there is a very large body of public opinion strongly in favour of the Wheat Board, and a unanimous body of public opinion strongly in favour of whatever finding is going to be the most beneficial to this Dominion. I am in no way opposed to the wheat pool, compulsory or voluntary. I am looking for information from the witnesses as to which method would reflect the greatest benefit to this Dominion. If it reflects benefit on the wheat grower and is indirectly reflected beneficially on the rest of the Dominion, that is a good thing, and that is the point we would like decided.
Now, listen, Mr. Speaker, to the answer:
I am afraid, Sir, that I have not a sufficiently decided opinion to advise you one way or the other.
This was the star witness brought by the protagonists of the Wheat Board before the Agricultural Committee. Let us now listen to what his partner, Mr. Riddell, said:

Wheat Board
ure that will establish a wheat board which those who know more about the matter than any one else say will be ineffective?
I feel, Mr. Speaker, not false but real modesty in talking to western grain growers about wheat. But I ask myself the question, why is it that the visible supply in Canada is not the sole determining factor in Canadian prices? The answer is found in the fact that Canada is not the only country in the world that grows wheat to fill the world's bread basket. During the months of January, February and March wheat from Australia and the Argentine republic goes on the world'f markets, and that is one reason why it may be wise for the Canadian grain grower of the West not to withhold his wheat from sale during, say, September and October, because if the crops are very abundant in Australia and the Argentine that may tend to depress the price in Canada during the months of the early winter. They also ship in smaller quantities during the summer months. In May, June and July India and Egypt ship wheat, and in Texas the harvest comes on in June. I suppose that the harvest there is commencing shortly. Then it comes northward at the rate of about 20 miles a day up to and through Canada. Kansas wheat is harvested in June. In looking at the grain reports the other day in the paper I saw a statement to the effect that the prices in Canada had dropped because it was expected that there would be a very excellent crop in Kansas. If you will remember, only a few weeks ago Mr. Watts, one of the witnesses, told us-I thought he took a certain unholy pleasure in the fact-that prospects in Kansas were bad and we might expect higher prices for Canadian wheat. The harvest in Kansas is substantial, amounting in 1921 to 128,000,000. Then Nebraska reaps her harvest after Kansas; Minnesota in August, then South Dakota, North Dakota, and so on into Canada. The world does not get its supplies all in a few months. The world gets its supplies not from hand to mouth, but from month to month throughout the year, and contracts months before for the supplies it is going to use. When a great deal of wheat in western Canada goes on the market in the early autumn months, much of it must have been sold before it was more than three or four inches from the ground. I would say that, although supply and demand is the ultimate determining factor in the establishment of price,
the demand is immensely influenced, not merely by the supply that is in sight, but by the judgment of buyers as to what the supply will be, not alone at the time in question but in the months that lie ahead. Hon. gentlemen who belong to the Agricultural Committee will remember how one witness, I think Mr. Richardson, stated that he might be buying wheat and paying certain prices for it on the exchange in the morning that at noon he might take up his paper and find that there had been abundant showers in Australia, and by reason of that fact change his attitude to the market during the afternoon. Is such a business as that is it wise that it should be under the control of a government? I do not think so. I think it is one in which personal initiative and insight should have full scope and play.

tion which my hon. friend has just brought to my attention. Mr. Richardson said:
Considerable wheat has been sold to the British buyer during the month of March.
He was giving his evidence on the 26th April.
Recently he has bought grain at values very much higher than he could have bought it last fall. He could have bought wheau for May and June shipment last fall just as readily as he can now, and he could have bought it for a great deal less money.
But what are the facts of the case? The English and foreign buyer does not appear to think that we give our wheat away in the fall of the year because he only buys his current requirements. Now, how can we account for this? It must be that he expected to buy cheaper from the Argentine after Christmas, or he does not watt to load up with our wheat in the fall of the year and run the risk of having his Canadian purchases show him a sharp loss should the Australian and Argentine crop be bountiful and come on the .market early in the New Year at lower prices.
Of course, it is quite possible that with Russia out of the market, if the Canadian crop was a very light one the prices would rise. I do not pretend for a moment that our wheat crop is not a big factor in the situation as far as determining prices is concerned, but I do give as my considered opinion to the members of this House that my study of this question has led me to the conclusion that although the wheat crop of Canada does come on the market in very large quantities during the months of September, October and November, the consequence is not to bear down the price, but that the prices realized during those fall months as a rule, taking one year with another and eliminating those abnormal years through which we have gone in the immediate past, pay the Canadian wheat grower to sell his wheat during those months. That is the conclusion to which I have come, and therefore when I am told that the banker to whom the grain grower owes money urges him to sell his wheat in September or October, I cannot blame the banker because I think he is asking his debtor to realize his property at the best price.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext: Is it your contention that the wheat comes on the world's market with regularity from almost every quarter of the globe?

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
No. I would say that wheat is largely grown in temperate climes, and that the North American continent and Russia being in the northern temperate clime have a larger production of wheat than similar countries to the south in a

southern temperate clime. I do not pretend that wheat is not a northern as opposed to a southern product. But the figures which I have studied lead me to the conclusion that the price of wheat is not determined merely by the Canadian supply coming on the market in September, October and November, and that the prices realized during those months, comparing them with a similar period six months thereafter are better prices than in the latter period.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
Could you explain
the newspaper quotations of to-day as to cash price and futures? The Winnipeg price quoted yesterday for No. 1 Northern was $1.29J cents. I notice the July quotations for futures are $1,221, but for October they are $1.14, and for December $1.12. Can you explain that situation?

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
No, I cannot. I think a man to give an adequate explanation of that situation would have to be far more familiar with the grain trade than I am. But my point is that the present system of competitive buying-for I believe the buying in Canada is competitive-is a good system. I believe the answer of Mr. James Richardson. I listened with interest to what he said, and I noticed the effect he made on my fellow-members in the committee. He said that he knows of no business which is conducted on as keenly a competitive basis as the export business of wheat, and that his company, which has been established for two generations, is in the closest and keenest competition with great houses in London, Paris and Rotterdam. You will remember he cited an instance where he had been competing with a rival for an order, and finally found that his competitor had got the order by having shaved his price a quarter of a cent per bushel. He did not understand how that could happen until he found there had been just that reduction in the freight rate, and that some one in the office of the shipping company had tipped off his competitor as to the probable reduction, which enabled that competitor to underbid him to that extent. I came to this matter with very little knowledge of the wheat business indeed and, I grant you, with a strong bent of mind against paternalism and paternal legislation, but I trust that did not prevent me dealing fairly and honestly with the evidence. It does seem to me that the way wheat is handled on the Winnipeg grain exchange by competitive buyers and com-

Wheat Board
petitive sellers does give as good results as would be given by pooling, though I am not opposed to pooling on the voluntary system, which I will deal with in a moment.
There have been many investigations into the wheat business. Mr. Richardson quoted an extract from a report made by a royal commission appointed by the Saskatchewan government, the closing words of the report being:
No doubt some bold and fortunate speculative exporters, and some large operators having the best of financial and shipping connections and favourable contracts for lake and ocean space make very good profits, but the commission has no evidence to indicate that the usual margin on which the exporting of wheat is conducted exceeds from one-half to one cent a bushel.
And Mr. Richardson told us that the profit of his business for the six months ending the 31st January was la slight fraction over g cent a bushel, or just about what this royal commission found.
Now, will the co-operative pool be of real advantage? That is something on which I do not wish to offer any advice; it is a matter which has to be decided by the western agriculturists themselves. But I would point out that co-operation in the past, so far as I know, never asked the State to come in to aid it in forming the co-operating body. It does seem to me that when the protagonists of the wheat board say: "We are not in favour of a co-operative pool because we do not believe there is enough co-operative sentiment in western Canada to form such a pool or to keep the members of such a co-operative society in it once it is formed; therefore we must invoke state aid to bring that desideratum about,"-I say that is the strongest argument against the interference of the state in that regard.

speechtext: I do not know whether I understood my hon. friend aright, but did he say that he knew of no co-operative enterprise which had had government assistance to establish it?

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
No, I did not say
that. What I did say was that I knew of no co-operative institution which had called upon the powers of the state to force people into the co-operation. That is the point I make, and if I may be allowed to say so-being, like most people of Scotch descent, a modest man-I think it is a strong one.

May I ask what are all our municipal enterprises if they
