speechtext:
Regina (Mr. Motherwell), who are leaders in a co-operative movement which took a strong stand against the great abuses which in the past had throttled the economic life of the western prairies.
I think it is dangerous to give the grain trade of a country into the hands of two or three men. If they deal rightly, if they judge rightly; if, I might almost say, they guess rightly, they may make a great deal of money for the country. If their judgment is wrong, if they make a mistake, then that mistake may result in great loss to the country.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext: Does the hon. member not realize that it is in the hands of two or three men now?

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
No; if hon. members can show that the grain trade of this country is in the hands of two or three men now they will not convert me to their proposal for compulsion-I do not think anything will do that-but they will make out a strong case for a voluntary pool. I do not, however, think that the grain trade is in the hands of two or three persons. I believe that the grain trade is subject to competition; if I am wrong, that part of my argument falls. But I would point out that under present circumstances one man may think that the market is going up; another man may think it is going down; and the net result will be much more on a level than if you put the whole grain trade of the country in the hands of two or three men. If you do that; if you put it in the hands of two or three men, you will get a dominant mind and that dominant mind will direct the whole trade of the country. I do not think it is reasonable or right; I do not think it is a fair risk to run, to put the whole grain trade of this country, which is our greatest individual trade, in the hands of one man. I think it is unfair to the present organization. Those who advocate a wheat board advocate it not as a permanent measure but as a temporary expedient; but even as a temporary expedient the upsetting of present organizations will result. I think it is unfair, or may prove to be unfair, to eastern Canada,-and this is the only note of a personal character that I will sound. I try in this House not to consider public matters from the mere point of view of the little county in the Eastern Townships which I represent, because I hold that we are here to consider the interests of Canada as a whole; we are here, elected from certain parts of

Canada, but our first duty is to the whole country. That was discussed in the English House of Commons as early as 1571; it was then laid down as the proper principle, and I believe it is the proper principle. Let me say this concerning eastern Canada; it is our desire to have as much of the wheat of this country as possible go out in the form of flour. It will be the duty of any wheat board that is doing anything of value to the west to try to put that wheat out just in the way in which it will give the greatest return to the western grower, irrespective of whether it goes out in wheat or in flour.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext: Is there anyone who is more entitled to all the returns that can be got from the wheat than the man who raised it?

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
No, there is not; if my hon. friend had waited just a moment I would have dealt with that aspect of the question. I am prepared to see the grower get whatever economic laws will give him. But I say it is not right for the state to interfere with economic law in order that certain wheat which otherwise would have gone out of this country in the form of flour shall go out in the form oi wheat. To the extent that that is done the eastern dairy farmer suffers.
I would say also that the adoption of such a proposal as this would create an enormously bad precedent. If it is right to have a wheat board, why not a potato board, why not a butter board? I know there are some men in this House who are so obsessed with the injustice and the ugliness of our present competitive individualistic system that they say, " Away with it; we can have no hope under it." I do not blame such men; I do not wonder at their advocacy of a wheat board. But men who follow the business of farming, men whose business is built up on personal initiative and on personal thrift-how they could advocate a wheat board which says to certain farmers who do not wish to enter it: " Whether you wish to enter this wheat board or not; whether you wish to pool the results of your labour and your capital with us or not, you have got to do it and the state will see that every avenue for the sale of your wheat except that which the state has created is closed to you,"

how they could advocate such a proposal as that, I cannot understand for it is striking at the very foundation of everything they hold dear.

Wheat Board
I would like to close with just one appeal to the protagonists of the wheat board. They all come from the West, and they, Mr. Speaker, and myself have for many years held in common certain great economic principles.
We have held these economic principles, we have been called idealists and impractical folk and we have suffered all sorts of things, if not at the hands, at least at the tongues of our fellow citizens; but those of us in the East who have held these principles have always looked to the West for hope and encouragement. The people of the West believe in fiscal freedom; they wish it for themselves; they wish it for their children. Let them not by the advocacy of this proposal, which is an interference with trade-it is not protection, but it is an interference with and an infraction of free trader-weaken their efforts to get what I believe will help them in the struggle for economic justice in which all the plain and common people of this country should be united as one man.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext: I shall only take up the time of the House for a few minutes. I asked a question of the pundit from Brome as to Joseph, and he could not answer my argument that Joseph had saved Egypt and the world at that time through his foresight, because of his violation of economic truths according to the hon. gentleman.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
The hon. member
forgets that we have now public ownership of railways and of ships, and if there was a famine we could bring wheat in from abroad.

subtopic: REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
The hon.
gentleman's argument was that this proposal would put the farmers in bondage, just as Joseph put the people of his day in bondage. Joseph saved Egypt and Moses saved the Israelites, and if there is any argument to be drawn from what these two great leaders did, it is that the foresight of Joseph and the patriotism of Moses saved humanity at these two stages of the world's history.
I am rather surprised that no reference has been made in this discussion to what is going on at Washington at the present time. The most powerful political organization that has been found anywhere in the world is operating to-day at Washington to secure some measure of relief from the farming conditions that exist in the western states of the American Republic, and they are coming to the same conclusion
that the Progressives are reaching in connection with their economic problems in the West. They are finding out in Washington that what is essential is that the credit of the nation, through the federal reserve banking system, shall be put behind some central organization for the purchase and the control and the sale, if necessary, of farm products, especially of wheat. We have come to it. We made a success of it in the late war, just as Joseph did. I think it would be a good thing to continue it; I believe in that; I believe in the credit of the nation being behind it. I believe in what the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) said about getting back to normal. The grievance of the farmers in the West is with the conditions they have encountered in normal times. Their experience in connection with the production of farm products in this country is such that they are prepared to try something else, and there will have to be a wheat board, with the credit of the nation behind it. There will have to be an elaborate system of storage in order to stabilize or valorize prices, and it may be necessary, in order that the farmer may get what is coming to him, that a crop like wheat may have to be stored for t>wo or three years ir. order to equalize the price and to keep the farmer in the meantime from being exploited by the gambler. The gambler in wheat, more than anything else, is the menace to farmers getting a fair price for their wheat, and the greatest gamblers in wheat are the millers and the banks which are associated with them in that proposition. That is what they are finding out in the states, and my hon. friend from Brome had better read the evidence that is being presented to-day in Washington if he wishes to see to what conclusions the farmers in the United States are coming. They are going to try something new. We have had two or three years' experience with the wheat board, and I say it is worth a continued trial. The president and the majority of the Senate in the United States are now in favour of rather extensive legislation in the direction of market control and the public control of the price of wheat, and are favouring putting the credit of the whole nation behind it.
When I addressed the House on the budget the other day I brought out this fact, that the coming thing for the improvement of agriculture in this country is improved transportation, improved national banking, improved marketing, and the introduction of the new principle of democ-
Wheat Board

racy and of economics, and that is collectivism. If the men in politics to-day go into the next election, when it comes, ignoring the principle of collectivism, or collective bargaining, call it what you will, by people who are dissatisfied with their present conditions and are going to try and help themselves by co-operation, collective bargaining, collective judgment, or a collective policy, they do not see the signs of the times.
There is just one other thing I want to say. We have the best wheat in the world grown in this country. There is no wheat like the Canadian wheat, and no wheat ought to command a higher price in the markets of the world. But the 'business has to be well handled. The gambler has to be eliminated, the high rate of interest has to be eliminated, and cheap transportation must be provided.. When my hon. friend from Brome says, "Do not offend the East," my answer is, who to-day in the East is standing at the door and telling not only the farmers of western Canada, but all the people of Canada, that they shall not have improved transportation by means of waterways so that steamships crossing the Atlantic may sail right up to the ports on the Great Lakes? The attitude of these grain speculators is: You shall not even have the advantage of the competition of sea-going ships. You farmers of the West must depend hereafter on the railroads, although water transport is cheaper.
In conclusion, I would ask the Prime Minister when he is drafting his bill to read the evidence that is now being presented to that committee in Washington. I have looked through it, and it deals with the question of marketing, with the question of financing crops, and with the question of storage. Storage is the real point, the strength of the farmers case. It does not cost much to store or to carry grain. There must be more storehouse capacity and the nation has to provide especially for the farmers of the West. We must have more storehouses, and the farmers must have granaries at home; they must have more local elevators and storehouses, and there may have to be great storehouses established at the seaports. I am quite convinced that the people of the United States, and especially the farmers of that country, hope to get a solution of the troubles that afflict the farmer over there, because they have troubles in the States just as we have them here. Over there they are trying to remove them, and

trying to do so by co-operation. The best thought in Congress, the best thought in the Senate is being devoted to this question, and the President of the United States is deeply concerned with it. They propose a great national movement over there to improve the price of farm products, to remove all kinds of gambling chances in them, and to provide storage for farm products-not only of wheat but of all grain, cotton and things of that kind. They are in favour of these things, and most of all they are in favour of making experiments. Now the greatest thing in politics is not to respect so-called economic laws but to make experiments. An experiment in politics is a great thing to try out; and as far as I am concerned I am willing to vote in favour of our Government establish-.ng a wheat board, of giving it all the assistance it can, and of having a real experiment made for a few years; especially in view of the fact that the Americans are going to make the same experiment. I believe that if we do make the experiment, having the best wheat in the world, we will be able, by some system of co-operation so to store and finance this good wheat of ours, that we can sell it at the highest price provided we exercise good judgment in that direction.

speechtext:

subtopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext: On motion of Hon. Sir Lomer Gouin (Minister of Justice) Bill No. 125 to amend the Supreme Court Act was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Most of the provinces have legislation to authorise references on legal questions to be made to their courts. There is no provision in the Supreme Court Act authorizing an appeal on such decision from the highest courts of the provinces. We were requested by the Attorney-General of Ontario to prepare the
[Deputy Speaker.]
amendment we now introduce. I would ask permission to make some changes in the amendment as drafted. I propose to replace in the first section, subsection 42 (a), for the words "Divisional Court of the Supreme Court of any province, (or by the final court of appeal of any province) ", the words "The highest Court of final resort in any province." This - is in conformity with the amendments made to the Supreme Court Act in 1920. For the same reason I move to strike out the words "Divisional Court (or of the said final court of appeal)", and to substitute therefor the words "the highest Court of final resort." This will apply to all the provinces of Confederation and I think it will be generally satisfactory.

subtopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: What is the purpose of the amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: To afford an appeal from the highest court of the province on any reference made in virtue of provincial legislation on questions of law. On federal matters we have references to the Supreme Court. The provincial governments have similar references to their provincial courts, but they have no appeal to the Supreme Court unless we amend the Supreme Court Act, and that is what we propose to do.

subtopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: At their request?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: At their request.

subtopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I notice it is intended by subsection 2 to make this bill retroactive to the 16th June, 1920.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SUPREME COURT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That subsection is dropped.
Bill reported as amended, read the third time, and passed.

subtopic: MILITIA AND DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
I had hoped, in common with most members of the late government, that we were getting near the end of these extraordinary payments. There is only a very small decrease this year, and I would ask the minister to be good enough to give the committee details of how this amount of $7,000,000 odd is made up.

Militia and, Defence
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Militia and Defence): We all shared my hon. friend's hope, but there does not seem much prospect that this item will be very materially diminished this year. Last year the vote was approximately $7,000,000, but about $8,000,000 was spent, the reason being that the Militia Department had several credits, and the Finance Department allowed that over-expenditure on account of those credits. It was really a matter of bookkeeping.

subtopic: MILITIA AND DEFENCE
speechtext:
I suppose that extraordinary large claim of $3,000,000 was charged up to the demobilization vote last
year?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: MILITIA AND DEFENCE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MILITIA AND DEFENCE
speechtext: Then do you not think this is too great a vote this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: MILITIA AND DEFENCE
speechtext:
Since these estimates
were prepared a credit of approximately $1,000,000 has been made by the British Shipping Board to the Naval Department, so this vote can be reduced to that extent.

subtopic: MILITIA AND DEFENCE
speechtext:
Does the minister mean that because Great Britain has paid us $1,000,000 in connection with war matters it can be used by the department without being covered by a vote?
Mr. GRAHAM. As a matter of fact, the British Shipping Board owed us $1,000,079, and gave us credit for it. Last year the Militia Department expended $1,000,000 more than the total voted by Parliament through credit given by that contra account. I will read the items that make up this total. One large item is that referred to by the ex-Minister of Militia last week, being the claim made by the British Shipping Board against the Canadian government, amounting to about $4,000,000, on account of the hospital ship that was sunk while being used by this government. The former Minister of Militia had some negotiations with the British government, but no final settlement was reached. I may say frankly that I have not had time to go into the merits or demerits of the case, but the $1,000,000 is credited against that claim. These are the items included in this vote: British Ministry of Shipping account, $3,007,105; private steamship accounts, $427,895; unforseen railway-steamship accounts, $200; other transportation claims, $40,000; separation allowances, $158,000; pay and allowances, $192,000;
war service gratuities, $346,000; printing and stationery, $26,000; postage on medals, records, etc., $60,000; ordnance service repairs to rifles, $6,000. Then there is an item for engineer services and works, $30,-
000.	There is a large amount for medals, $535,000. These medals are made by the British government and are paid for by the Canadian government. I may say to hon. members whose friends may be asking why their medals or other decorations have not reached them that they are coming into the department by thousands every month and we are distributing them as rapidly as they are received. There are items for difference in exchange redeemed at par, $86,500, and miscellaneous, unforeseen, $470,000, making a total of $6,880,-
000.	We add to that the $500,000 we discussed the other night, for battlefields memorials, making a total of $7,380,000. As I pointed out a moment ago we wish to drop $1,000,000 from that, leaving the amount to be voted $6,380,000.

subtopic: MILITIA AND DEFENCE
speechtext:
The amount
of $470,000 for miscellaneous unforseen expenses strikes me to be rather a large item, and I would like the minister to give us some particulars concerning it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: MILITIA AND DEFENCE
speechtext: It is to cover any items not otherwise provided for which may be authorized by the Governor in Council. There is also a balance in dispute, a claim of Vickers Limited, of $219,000. Then, a committee is sitting at present the recommendations of which may necessitate some expenditure. There were upwards of 6,000 soldiers who took their discharge from the Canadian forces in England, many of whom have since come to Canada. The question of refunding the cost of their transportation to Canada has been before the special committee on pensions and soldiers' re-establishment. The amount involved is estimated at $330,000. Provision is made to cover these two items. In fact, . in connection with the committee which is sitting, my fear is that I may have to ask for a supplementary vote to cover any provision the committee may make for payments, and so on.

subtopic: MILITIA AND DEFENCE
speechtext:
I agree that
my hon. friend has not allowed very much to cover the recommendations of the committee; the amount would appear to be $231,000. I would like to ask how the claim of the Vickers Company stands at present.

Militia and Defence

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: MILITIA AND DEFENCE
speechtext:
It has not yet been
settled. There have been some negotiations; I have gone over the file of figures once or twice, and I think my predecessor discussed the claim with the Vickers people when 'he wad in England. The claim must, of course, be paid in some amount, but a definite decision has not been arrived at.

subtopic: MILITIA AND DEFENCE
speechtext:
I do know something about this claim. I went into the matter fully when I was in the department and I was not able to effect a settlement with the Vickers people. They made an offer to accept a certain sum of money to clean up the whole claim. I at one time thought the figure Was not an unfair one, but my hon. friend the then Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) thought it was much too high. I am satisfied that the company have a bona fide claim. We cancelled certain contracts which we had awarded to them at the beginning of the war and they claim to have sustained losses. Some substantial amount will have to be paid in settlement of this claim. But the large item which the minister has given is the one that I would like a little more information about, that is, the one in connection with the shipping claim of the British government against the Canadian government. I was under the impression that last summer, with the able assistance of accountants from the Militia Department and after about three weeks' hard work, we reached a settlement with the British government, of their claims against Canada in regard to all shipping items save one. We succeeded in reducing the account which had been rendered to us by $750,000. But there was still a very large item in regard to a hospital ship that had been torpedoed and in respect of which the British government claimed they had the right to recover from Canada the amount found to be due to the owners by a board of arbitration which sat in England and was made up of three or four prominent ship owners. Upon that board Canada was not represented. In the early stage of the submarine warfare the damages paid by the British government to British ship owners were based on the actual cost of the ship. But as the war proceeded and more and more ships were sunk every month, the cost of shipbuilding rapidly went up and in the later years of the war the boards of arbitration awarded the replacement value of the ships. The British ship in question was in the service of Canada at the time she was lost. Marine insurance rates had become so [Sir Henry Drayton.I
great that no government could carry them; a few months' insurance would eat up the whole value of the ship. Canada, having assumed the risk while the vessel was under charter to her, has been called upon to make good the loss occasioned through the vessel having been torpedoed. My recollection is that the cost of the ship is about $1,000,000 and that the finding of the board of arbitration was that we should pay a replacement value of something like $3,000,000, I think-an enormous figure, at all events. These figures will be found in the department. Last summer we were not able to arrive at an agreement in regard to that item. In reply to my objection that Canada was not represented on the arbitration board, the officials of the Ministry of Shipping said that men had been appointed whom they thought would represent us; that the same board had acted in reference to British, Australian and Canadian ships, ships of every nation, and they were under the impression that Canada was virtually bound by the arrangement. I took the other ground, so the matter stood. But all other outstanding items in regard to shipping were settled, and the document setting forth the settlement must be in the department. I have the impression that the amount was not nearly so great as that stated by my hon. friend to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: MILITIA AND DEFENCE
speechtext: My hon. friend is right; I have the figures here. Settlement was made of all the other claims, but the amount has not been paid, so it comes under this vote. We have to take $2,243,000 from this item for that purpose. That comes out of this amount to begin with.

subtopic: MILITIA AND DEFENCE
speechtext: The claim, I think, was three and a quarter million, and they reduce it to about two and a half million.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: MILITIA AND DEFENCE

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service

subtopic: MILITIA AND DEFENCE
speechtext:
I would like to urge upon the minister the desirability of having these war medals distributed to those entitled to them at the earliest possible date. The men who are entitled to them value them very highly, but if they do not get them soon, they will probably care very little about them. The war is over now almost four years, and I think it is desirable that the distribution of medals should be speeded up. I have received many requests about


Militia and Defence
them, as no doubt have other hon. members, and I would suggest that if it is a question cf manufacture, that the manufacture be speeded up. If it is simply a question of distribution, an effort should be made to get the medals out as soon as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: MILITIA AND DEFENCE
speechtext: The department receives a great many requests too. For a time the department was sending out as many as 25,000 medals a month. We are sending them out now just as rapidly as we get them. We are in communication with the British authorities urging them to speed up production. Just as fast as we get them, we distribute them. The young men and their relatives are naturally getting very anxious to get the medals. Our list is all ready, and we have quite a large staff that is being retained largely for the purpose of distributing these medals. I can assure my hon. friend that we are doing everything possible to speed up the manufacture at the other end.

subtopic: MILITIA AND DEFENCE
speechtext: I think the record of the department in regard to the distribution of medals is pretty good, when you consider the millions of medals that have to be made for all the men who served in the army and navy of Great Britain and the Dominions. I enquired into this matter last summer and found that they were speeding up in every possible way, but I suppose there must be eight or ten million medals altogether to be made and distributed.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: It is to provide for cleaning machinery in the elevator at Vancouver so as to put that elevator in a position to handle grain, more particularly the grain coming in over the Canadian National Railways. Considerable grain was shipped there during the winter, I think around eight million bushels, and it may be interesting to the committee to know that from the province of Alberta it is cheaper to ship grain to England via Vancouver than via the Atlantic ports.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: May I ask the minister what has been done to meet the need for terminal elevators in the province of Ontario? About three years ago there waited upon the government a large deputation composed of the following representatives: City of Toronto, Minister of Agriculture for Ontario, United Farmers' of Ontario, United Farmers' Co-operative Company, Limited, representatives of the Grain section, Toronto Board of Trade, representatives of the Toronto Harbour Commission. The deputation introduced asked that an interior elevator be built in Ontario and we presented a very elaborate memorandum to the government showing the necessity for it. I would like to ask the minister if the time has not come to consider the policy of building one or more of these elevators in the province of Ontario? The government told us in 1918 they would build one when the war was over. At present there are no such facilities in central and western Ontario for the storage of the farmer's crop. It was pointed out that in some cities a large expenditure is being made on harbour improvements. In my own city we used to have these elevators some years ago but now we have not got any. $26,000,000 is being spent rebuilding the port. The urgent need of an elevator at some place on lake Ontario, has been pointed out. I would like to know if anything is going to be done in this direction for the province of Ontario because the government has established elevators in other parts of the country and I think they should do the same for the province from which I come?

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: As my hon. friend is surely aware there is a greater storage capacity in the province of Ontario than in any of the other provinces. He must be cognizant of the immense storage capacity we have at Fort William and Port Arthur, and I suppose the province of Ontario will claim that those two enterprising towns are within its boundaries. At Port Colborne there is also a large elevator, and there are likewise elevators at Georgian Bay ports. So far as I am aware no complaint has been received of the shortage of storage capacity on the lakes.

speechtext:
I am going to read from the memorandum presented by the deputation referred to, a few paragraphs with respect to the need of terminal elevators in Ontario, because I am satisfied the minister is not seized of the very im-

Grain Elevators
portant facts embodied1 therein: The purpose of the deputation was thus stated:
The purpose of the deputation is to ask the government of Canada to erect and operate an interior termtinal elevator for the service of Ontario, particularly central and western Ontario. It is assumed that such an elevator would be included as one of the chain of elevators at (present operated by the Board of Grain Commissioners of the Department of Trade and Commerce. The type of elevator should, it is submitted, follow the lines of those at present in operation at Calgary, Saskatoon and Moosejaw in the western provinces, and be modern and well equipped in every particular. Its capacity should be sufficient to meet the needs of central and western Ontario as determined after examination by the experts of your departments. Such an elevator, it is submitted, should be located where convenient transportation facilities are available by road, by rail and by water. While we realize that the selection of the exact location would be contingent on the investigation of the experts of your departments, we are glad to have associated with us in this deputation representatives of the Toronto Harbour Commission Board.
Ontario produces annually approximately 200,000,000 bushels of grain of various kinds. In 1918 the total aggregated nearly 225,000,000 bushels, but this was an exceptionally favourable year for grain crops. It will be seen that in the average year Ontario produces enormous quantities of grain. Very considerable of this grain is used for live stock feeding as the live stock industry is a prominent one in the province of Ontario. At the same time there is no doubt but that millions of bushels change hands each year as grain, being sold either in the local trade, in inter-provincial trade, or for export. At the present time there Is no Government interior terminal elevator in the province at which grain may be officially weighed and graded, as is done m the other provinces. At the present time the Grain Commission is endeavouring to purchase over 500,000 bushels of oats in Ontario, but there is no central point at which this grain can be officially asembled, weighed and graded. The absence of these facilities in Ontario has proven a loss to the farmers, a great inconvenience to those engaged in the grain trade, and a handicap to the Province in competing in these lines with other provinces which have the benefit of such facilities.
This deputation, therefore, desires to lay special emphasis on the public service functions which such an elevator would perform to the agricultural and commercial Interests of the province.
Then follows a summary of the functions alluded to among which appear the following:
It would provide accommodation for the weighing, cleaning, drying, storing and grading of all kinds of grata in the province.
It would be an advantage to individual farmers, by enabling them to ship carload lots of grain which would be officially weighed and stored, and for which there would be issued an official certificate which would be recognized by the bank at once, thus broadening the farmers' market.
It would provide facilities for the storing, cleaning and grading of different kinds of seed
and in this regard would be of great advantage to the farmers of the province, particularly with reference to grass and clover seeds.
It would be of much advantage to the live stock industry of the province by facilitating the distribution of feeding stuffs from one section to another in the case of short crops in the local districts or In the province as a whole.
It would be able to perform a distinct service in preventing the deterioration of certain crops in the province in the years of too much moisture, as is illustrated in the bean crop in recent years. The crop of buckwheat this year has had to be dried because of the wet weather which prevailed at the time of harvsting.
Special emphasis is laid on the fact that such an elevator would be a public elevator and certificates issued would be official government certificates, both of which are advantages affording great protection to the public and not available in the same sense from private enterprise.
Then the commercial side of the question is dwelt upon in the memorandum and the great advantages that would result from the carrying out of the enterprise are effectively pointed out.

I hope the minister will look into this matter, because I have in my possession a very elaborate brief which has been carefully prepared by the interests that I have named. I know the late Lieutenant-Governor Clark was a man who took a great deal of interest in the farming and grain interests of Ontario, and he was very much seized with the importance of having proper terminal elevators, because the steam railways are not treating the farmers of the province as they should and the fact is that the farmers have no place to take their crop in western and central Ontario. I have a large number of petitions signed by men interested in farming exhibitions, fairs and so on. We have been told that the financial situation has been such that public works could not be built except where absolutely necessary; but for the last year or two the financial situation has been improving, and I hope the minister will give us some relief. I have petitions signed

Grain Elevators

by county councils and various other public bodies that I have named. It is too bad that, in the old province of Ontario, we are not getting the relief that we should get even as regards elevator transportation facilities. On account of the fact that we could not get proper transportation facilities from the steam roads, 368 municipalities became so disgusted with the way they were being treated by the steam roads that they passed bylaws for a large system of hydro-electric railways in Ontario. We are quite agreeable that more elevators should be built throughout the country; but in Ontario they seem to have been eliminated. True it is, that there is one at Fort William and another at Port Colborne; but they are for through waterborne traffic largely, and western Ontario and central Ontario are absolutely lacking in elevator facilities to take care of the farmers' grain crops. We have a very active and aggressive minister; I hope he will take this matter up and give us some relief in central and western Ontario. I do not wish to detain the committee, and I would like to see these estimates go through quickly. I hope the minister will go into this very important matter, meet this deputation again and see if something cannot be done to give the farmers of western and central Ontario a place to store their crop. Why should Ontario not have at the country's expense what every other province has now?

speechtext: I should like to offer a suggestion to the minister regarding the administration of these terminal elevators, and I think my suggestion might appropriately come under this item. At present the administration of terminal elevators owned by the Government, both at the head of the lakes and at points further west, lies in the hands of the Grain Commission. One of the commissioners, indeed, has active charge of the administration of these elevators. I have always thought that was a mistake as regards administration. The Grain Commission is a judicial body created by act of this Parliament for settling disputes that may arise in the conduct of the grain business. It was never intended to be an administrative board in the sense of administering the operation of these elevators. My suggestion to the Government and to the minister-and I am sure it will receive his usual careful consideration-is that his department might well give consideration to the matter of separating the administration of these terminal elevators from the Board of Grain Commissioners altogether and putting the administration in charge of a competent official for that purpose. That would relieve the Board of Grain Commissioners of that duty; it would place them more clearly in the judicial capacity which they are supposed and intended under the act to occupy. As a matter of fact, the Government is operating terminal elevators in competition with private concerns. I have no fault to find with that. I have advocated in the past and I still adhere to the view that it might be better, in the interest of the whole tradte of Canada, if all these terminal elevators were operated as Government utilities the same as the Government elevator at Port Arthur is. But in any case, so long as they are operating an elevator, it should be an administrative function directly responsible to the minister and should not be involved with the conduct of a body that should be entirely judicial in its operations and character.

I should like to call the minister's attention to a matter regarding the car demurrage rule, which provides for forty eight hours' free time exclusive of Sundays for loading and unloading commodities. The exception to that rule is that, in that portion of Canada, Port Arthur and the West, in which the Grain Act applies, twenty hours' free time only is allowed for loading grain. I understand this legislation was enacted with a view to speeding up the loading and prompt handling of grain in the short time available for handling the crop. This legislation hits directly at the farmer; in fact, he is the only one hit, as the elevators have no limit to the number of cars they can load provided that they can get the cars. The farmer, on the other hand, unless he live**very close to an elevator, is unable to load a car in twenty-four hours, and as help is very hard to get at this time, he usually has to take an extra day to load his car. As a result, the handling of grain is not speeded up; in fact, in 95 cases out of 100 the farmer has to take 48 hours to load a car, and the object for which the rule was passed is not attained". For that

speechtext:
It is not exactly a resumption of that work, but as a result of that inquiry and what was brought out it was represented to us from some sources that there still existed some degree of unfairness, that the matter had not been all cleaned up to the satisfaction of the trade, and we therefore put in this vote to provide for any inquiry, should one be demanded. I may say at once that if there is a reasonable request from the growers for an investigation the Government will be disposed to consider it. Of course, we must bear in mind that there is no trade in this country that has been so often investigated as the grain trade of western Canada. I have been looking into the matter and I find that there have been thirteen different inquiries, royal commissions, and departmental investigations, into the trade of western Canada, and I suppose that an investigation is looked upon as an annual affair. I repeat, we are open to sugges-

tions from our friends who are interested in western Canada, and the Government will be guided by the representations that are submitted to them.

speechtext:
So far as the work of the Hyndman Commission is concerned, and the causes that led to the appointment of that body, I think it is pretty well within the knowledge of every one who knew anything of the circumstances, that there was no widespread demand,-indeed, as far as I know, there was no demand from any reasonable body of opinion-for the institution of that inquiry at the time it was started. I do not wish to-night to enter upon any extensive discussion of the work of the Hyndman Commission, so called, further than to make this observation, that it was very unfortunately constituted, in some of its personnel, for the work it had to do. I have stated publicly elsewhere, and I repeat here, that the late Commissioner Staples, of the Board of Grain Commissioners, should certainly never have been placed on any royal grain inquiry. There was no useful work that the royal grain inquiry, known as the Hyndman Commission, undertook to do that could not have been done by the Board of Grain Commissioners in the first instance. The Board of Grain Commisioners is expressly clothed under the law with all the powers of inquiry that are vested under part one of the Inquiries Act. I have stated before, and I will repeat here, that the main purpose of the Grain Enquiry Commission was political rather than to seek remedies for abuses in the grain business. However, that may pass now. 'So far as inquiries are concerned, I do think that the minister might well institute some investigation, departmental or otherwise, that would go fully and thoroughly into the operation of the terminal elevators at Fort William, covering the handling of grain from the time it enters those elevators until it leaves. The elevators at Fort William are under the direction and control of the Government in the matter of inspection and weighing. The supervision of the grain handled through these elevators is always under the eye of government officials, and consequently the certificate of weight or of grade issued on grain entering these elevators or leaving them is a government certificate. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Saltcoats (Mr. Sales), there has been a good deal of dissatisfaction, particularly in the past year, with the outward inspection at some of the elevators at Fort William.

Grain Commission
My own judgment is that the inspection work at Fort William has been weak, and not properly looked after. In that respect I have another suggestion to offer to the minister. It is that the whole work of grain inspection covered by the Canada Grain Act 'be placed in the hands of the chief grain inspector, who should be made responsible for the efficiency and character of this work throughout his jurisdiction. As a matter of fact, owing to conditions that existed in Fort William under the administration of the law-which I do not wish to enter into to-night to any extent- the inspection of the elevators was not as closely under the direction and control of the chief grain inspector as it should have been. Theoretically he may have been the official responsible for the efficiency of that inspection, but in actual practice a condition developed at the head of the lakes under which he did not have that control which he should have had. I think the causes for that condition probably do not now obtain, but in my judgment the minister would be well advised to place the whole inspection business under the chief grain inspector and make him responsible to the department instead of to the Board of Grain Commissioners, for the same reason that I urged a few moments ago that the administration of the terminal elevators should be taken out of the hands of the Board of Grain Commissioners. The business of grain inspection is an administrative function, and the best results will be obtained in the administration of this act if that function is disassociated from the judicial function which primarily rests, as it should rest, in the Board of Grain Commissioners.
There is another matter which I wish to make allusion to, because I find that throughout eastern Canada particularly there is a very widespread misunderstanding and misapprehension of the conditions existing in the terminal elevators, and especially in the elevator controlled by the company with which I have been associated. The Royal Grain Inquiry Commission early last June, when it was sitting in the province of Saskatchewan, by telegram authorized its secretary to hold a special session at Fort William, which was in the nature of a secret session. That session was held as was disclosed in evidence brought out in the injunction proceedings at Winnipeg, for the purpose of investigating certain charges against the Grain Growers' administration of their terminal
elevator. The inquiry was held in camera, no notice was given to the parties concerned, and very serious charges were levelled against the United Grain Growers for what had happened eight years previous. I repeat that this evidence was received and published in the newspapers throughout the country without our having any chance to appear at the proceedings and question the witness who gave that evidence, in which serious reflections were made on that company. It was the most unfair and unjudicial inquiry under the guise of a commission that has ever taken place in the Dominion. I wish to place these facts before the House and the country in order that they may appreciate what really took place.
The impression exists, and it was fostered in every possible way during the last election campaign, that the United Grain Growers were afraid of an inquiry into their administration; in a word, that there was something dark and mysterious and sinister that they wished to conceal. Within a few weeks of the time that that inquiry took place at Fort William we asked the Board of Grain Commissioners- who have practically all the powers that the Royal Grain Inquiry Commission had- to investigate as thoroughly and completely as they could all the allegations that had been made against the company. That was not done, although we repeated our request several times. We took the opportunity to clear up as far as we were able these allegations, and, speaking for that responsible company that has been doing business and enjoys a good reputation, I hope that if an inquiry is made by the minister it will cover the particular transactions that I have referred to, because there is no foundation in fact for the allegations which were made at this particular sitting. And, let me say again that secretly arranged session was one of the most discreditable episodes that has occurred in any judicial inquiry 4n the history of this country.
I think some useful purpose could be served by an inquiry into the operation of the terminal elevators. I believe that all the legitimate terminal elevators-and I make no reflections on any of the operators of those elevators-would welcome such an inquiry. I believe that the inspection at Fort William last year was lax, particularly in regard to outward business, but that was the fault of the administration
Grain Commission

of the law, and has led to the criticism referred to by some hon. members here as to the quality of our grain not being up to the standard of inspection when it reaches the markets of the world. It is of the very greatest importance to the farmers and others engaged in the wheat business in western Canada that the high reputation our grain has hitherto enjoyed should be maintained by keeping up the high standard of our inspection, and I have every confidence that this will be done by the chief grain inspector in Winnipeg. I have known him for many years as a man well qualified for the post he holds, and I am quite certain that if he is given the necessary authority he will see that the inspection of western Canadian wheat is kept up to the proper standard and will not permit monkeying with it in any elevator. It should be borne in mind, let me repeat, that the inspection and weighing of grain into and out of these elevators is altogether in the hands of government officials, and I believe if the minister accepts and puts into effect the suggestions I have offered him to-night it will result in placing the administration of those houses on a basis where every person desires to see it placed and maintained.
So far as an inquiry into the handling of grain through country elevators is concerned, it could do no harm, but I frankly say that I do not think any very useful results would accrue from it. If, however, there is a widespread demand for such an inquiry it should be granted. But I would point out again that the Grain Act expressly clothes the Board of Grain Commissioners with all the powers necessary to inquire into any complaints of abuses that may exist in the handling of grain anywhere throughout the three prairie provinces, and I think that board could do the work, and do it to the satisfaction of all the producers who are interested in the handling of grain.

I feel but ill prepared to talk about the grain business and the so-called iniquities of the grain inquiry, the impropriety of trying to find out whether or not allegations made are correct, especially at this late hour, and more particularly because I never was very intimately connected with these matters. However, I want to say one or two things. In the first place, let me tell my hon. friend (Mr. Crerar) that there were complaints and are complaints with regard to the manner in which the1 business is being carried on. It may be that as the operator of his terminal company these complaints are not heard by my hon. friend as they are by others. But I had complaints made to me to-day by one of his own followers with regard to the way the farmers are treated, True, he makes no specific complaint as against this elevator company or that, but the complaints are as to prices, as to treatments; they affect the farmer and the grower, particularly those at a distance from railways. He says that one day the price of wheat is so much; he is told he can get so much, but when he proceeds to try to get it he finds that the market has disappeared and he can find out nothing about it. If the leader of the third party, then, does not know that there were complaints, let me tell him that there were many complaints in western Canada as to grain handling, grain marketing, grain practices, and grain prices. There are complaints to-day, and he must know of them. I do not pretend for one minute to know anything about what was done by the Hyndman commission. But I want to say this: I have known my hon. friend for some time, and I was convinced when I saw that evidence that my hon. friend had nothing to do with it and knew nothing about it. But I thought he took the very worst step he could have taken in his own interests in

Grain Commission
saying that the lid had to ba put on; that at all hazards, whether the grain law of Canada was upset or not, the injunction should go and that this country and the grain trade should1 be put in the position in which it now is. Sometimes mistakes are made. In this case I think a great mistake was made, but without the slightest thought as to the consequences entailed; without the slightest thought on my hon. friend's part that he had done anything wrong that he would have to cover up. But it is a mistake when you are one hundred per cent right to put yourself in a position where people can say you are one hundred per cent wrong.

speechtext: They did not say that.

He did not say it, no; but when a charge is made, when evidence is disclosed pertaining to it and many people look upon the person charged as entirely innocent, the very last thing that will cause them to hold to that view is an injunction. Well, the inquiry was stopped. If I recollect aright, the court, notwithstanding everything my hon. friend has said to-day, held that the Hyndman Commission had a right to go on; that nothing had been done in Fort William or anywhere else which would prevent the board from functioning as it ought to function. My hon. friend says he is going to wait for complaints. Surely he knows there are complaints; surely he knows there was dissatisfaction. I am very glad to hear the leader of the third party suggest that an inquiry should be held; in fact, I should have thought he would have been absolutely insistent upon it. He says he finds there are suspicions abroad. That is quite right; and I hope they will be allayed. There were suspicions, and they were made all the worse by reason of the newspaper defence that was put in by the Grain Growers' Company. The defence which dealt with the question of sleeves made the situation all the worse. I hope, I say, they will all be got rid of and that my hon. friends will be able to show that they have had nothing whatever to do with it.
Now, the hon. member for Marquette insinuates that the whole object behind this inquiry was a political one. Well, I know some people do make political footballs of grievances. But if in the carrying on of their business the farmers have had real difficulties, and if in that connection some one should try to find out what was wrong, the mere possibility of a political opponent
being in a position, to use the words of one of my hon. friend's own late colleagues, to "farm the farmer"-that, I contend, does not make any inquiry into those grievances entirely political. I venture to suggest that that is an improper position for my hon. friend to take; it is an unfair insinuation. Whatever investigation is made, I am confident that the honour of my personal friend will remain just where I have always felt it was. But for the protection of that honour, the very best thing that can be done is to continue that investigation which the courts of the country have found to be properly constituted.

I have only a word to say in reply to what the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) has just stated. I appreciate the reference he has made to myself; I could have wished that his political friends throughout Canada in the last election had entertained always the same opinion. So far as the work of the Hyndman Commission is concerned and its attitude in the particular instance that I mentioned, I want nothing more than the exposure of the whole facts to the fullest light of day so that they may be seen by every person in this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific. My hon. friend says that I was poorly advised when injunction proceedings were taken to restrain the commission; when the lid was put on. Why were the injunction proceedings taken? If my hon. friend were in similar circumstances and he believed and knew from all the facts of the case, as far as the facts of the case could inform him, that he could not get a fair judgment or a fair show from such a commission, what would he do? He would do precisely what was done in that case, and the best evidence of the fact that the United Grain Growers did not wish to put the lid on, but wished to have the full facts investigated, lies in this, that they asked the Board of Grain Commissioners who had all the powers necessary in the matter, to make a most thorough inquiry into the whole proceedings at Fort William. Instead of any desire to put on the lid, there was the fullest possible desire to have the whole thing exposed to the light of day, but exposed to the light of day in a fair manner, and not in a prejudiced manner. My hon. friend, whom I acquit at once-I am not in the slightest degree reflecting upon him-but let me remind him that not only did we ask that this question be investigated in the fullest possible manner by the Board of Grain Com-
Grain Commission

missioners, who had, let me repeat, all the powers necessary to investigate it, but my hon. friend's friends in western Canada made this matter an issue in the recent election in the prairie provinces. I could take him to the country school-houses and show him literature that was sent out by the hundreds of pounds from the publicity offices of his party in Winnipeg, Regina, and Calgary. The one issue submitted to the people by my hon. friend's friends in western Canada was that Progressives should not be supported, that Crerar was a dangerous man, that he had refused to have his case investigated, that he was under a cloud. These were the statements made by my hon. friend's friends in western Canada. As a matter of fact, not only did we not seek to evade any inquiry, but I repeat, my hon. friend's friends made this an issue m western Canada, and, Mr. Chairman, they got their reply on December 6th.
I do not wish to burk any inquiry. As far as I personally am concerned, and so far as the farmers' companies are concerned, they court the fullest possible inquiry. But I would say this: there have been grievances in western Canada. I have never known a year when there were not grievances, and often legitimate grievances, on the part of the farmers in the handling of their grain, but I ask again, why was the Board of Grain Commissioners created by the late government? It was created for the specific and sole purpose of inquiring into these grievances, and it did inquire into them. If a farmer could not get cars to ship his grain, or was getting unfair treatment from a country elevator, he could report to the Board of Grain Commissioners and under the law they were required to investigate his case, and when the facts warranted they did investigate his case. I regret to say that there grew up a condition in western Canada where there was a great lack of faith in the Board of Grain Commissioners, and I believe the cause of that lack of faith has lately been removed from the board.
This business should be put on a fair basis. I repeat, I think an inquiry could usefully be made in respect to the operation of terminal elevators in the manner I indicated a little while ago and I think the minister would be well advised in undertaking it. If there is a substantial reason why such an inquiry should go further into the prairies and investigate conditions there, I have no objection, but that involves expense. I say, again, if your Board of Grain Commissioners is properly

constituted, and I have a good deal of confidence in the board as it stands at present, they could inquire into all these things and settle them. The board was created for that purpose. The late government showed a great lack of faith in its own board when it did not entrust to them an inquiry into all these matters. I do not wish to make my language too strong. I try to be temperate and moderate in my statements in this House, but I will leave it to any reasonable man in this country whether the whole proceedings, the literature, disseminated by my hon. friend's party in western Canada during the election, literature that reached out into the far province of British Columbia, and the stories that I heard down in the maritime provinces, did not stamp the whole thing as largely political. My hon. friends to my right have certainly suffered a very great deal at the hands of some of their friends in the late contest.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I would ask the minister who are the members of the Board of Grain Commissioners at present?

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Mr. Boyd, Chairman, Mr. Jones, and we have lately appointed Mr. Matthew Snow, who seems to enjoy in a very large degree the confidence not only of the growers but the handlers of grain in western Canada.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I do not want to prolong this discussion at all. I want to be absolutely fair and frank. I think my hon. friend is sorry he ever got that injunction. I think he is sorry he upset the Grain Act of this country.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Not correct.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
After all the doubts and all the troubles we have had in connection with this recent legislation, which all flow from the work that was done in connection with these injunction proceedings, I am quite sure my hon. friend is sorry that he ever took that step. It strikes one as being so totally inconsistent that one should be so anxious to be tried by this same man when he is one-third of a court, and object to him when he is only one-fourth of the court. My hon. friend no doubt wants an investigation, and I agree that he should have it. I hope it will go on, and that it will be thorough, and I hope that the evidence that was given will be absolutely refuted to the fu:l one hundred per cent that it is possible to refute it. If by any chance it be true

Grain Commission
that there was in the elevator there-it does not make a bit of difference whose elevator it was-any false bottoms, false weighing machines, sleeves or any other artificial dodge by which it would be possible for the grain grower to be cheated, I hope that fact will be established.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
I have just one observation to make, and that is to point out to the committee that the validity of the Grain Act was questioned long before the injunction	proceedings	were	taken	inWinnipeg last summer. I do not want to detract in any way from whatever strength my hon. friend might bring to the support of a very weak case. But that is a fact that every	one	is well	aware	of:	The
validity of the Act was questioned before those injunction proceedings were taken.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: If that is so, I apologize; I did not know it.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
It is not my intention
to enter	into	the debate	that	hasinterested	the	House	seeing	that	the
laurels rest upon my leader. He has made the statement that often times in the West conditions obtain with which the farmer is not satisfied. Now during the marketing season the whole country is filled with complaints. It is true that some have not proven to be well founded, and others again have not perhaps much weight; but I want to state this-and I have a concrete instance before me to prove it-that it seems to me the grain companies in western Canada frequently take liberties that are not warranted. I may state further that perhaps the individual growers of wheat do not always appreciate the fact that a Board of Grain Commissioners exists for the purpose of investigating such evils as may be existing in the grain trade. Now the particular instance which I wish to cite to the House has to do with a neighbour of mine who shipped a carload of grain down to the terminal elevator with instructions to store the grain, and upon instructions later on to sell that grain he received the return. He sent a copy of it down to me and it seems to me that the company concerned has taken a most unwarranted license with that man's grain. For instance in this case when the grain was stored a wire was sent him advising him that the price was $1.26. Before leaving the station he sent a reply "Accept that price". I can quite conceive that in the time occupied in the transmission of that wire from Winnipeg to his station and the transmission of the reply,
there might be a drop in price; in fact the price did drop li cents. But this grain was in store for 93 days and I believe when it was put into the storage elevator it was cleaned. But the return shows that twenty-six bushels were cleaned out of that carload of grain and for those screenings this man was charged $2.29 storage. Now I do not believe that twenty-six bushels was stored because wheat is cleaned before storing, and yet we find that $2.29 is charged for storage alone for some twenty-six odd bushels cleaned out of that grain. Under the law screenings are sold as feed and computed by the ton and having paid $2.29 for storage my neighbour received just 33 cents for his twenty-six bushels. He absolutely lost the whole value of the screenings as feed, was charged $2.29 for the storage of cleanings which I believe never were stored, and he received only 33 cents. Now someone received that profit of $2.29; I believe that if the matter were pressed it can be proved that this is an unwarranted license and an injustice to (the man who owned the wheat. There are many very similar cases which I might quote, but I thought the recitation of the one instance would be sufficient. It does seem to me that an occurrence of this kind needs to be rectified and possibly it would be a wholesome lesson for companies that in the past-and I can confirm this by my own personal experience for years-take liberties with the grain which they have received for care and keeping. I simply wished to placed this matter on record as one instance of the things that are complained of.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: If my hon. friend from Assi-niboia will send the details of that particular instance to my office I will have it investigated.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: That is what the Board of Grain Commissioners exists for.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
I may say, on behalf of the Government, that we have but one desire and that is to restore confidence in the administration of the grain trade of Canada -we admit there is want of confidence-and also to ensure that the wheat of Canada will maintain its splendid reputation. It is unfortunately too true that in recent times the reputation of our grain has suffered somewhat. I want to tell my hon. friends from the West that no later than to-day, I met the correspondent of a western newspaper, and the western grain grower has no better friend1 than the correspondent in question, who has recently returned from
Grain Commission

the British Isles. He informed me that there is a suspicion over there that our grain is not exactly what it should be, more particularly the grain going out from ports other than Canadian. The trade of the country can help us along these lines. If we wish to ensure that our grain shall go out maintaining its splendid reputation is it not reasonable that we should use our own ports, thus giving the earnings to our own transportation companies? In that way we shall help to maintain1 the reputation of our own products. I am not desirous of delaying the passage of my own estimates, but I just wished to give this assurance to my hon. friend that if we have an investigation-and both opposition parties seem to be desirous that there should he an inquiry-we will grant the fullest and plainest investigation in order that absolute confidence in the administration of the grain trade may exist on the part of all those engaged in this industry.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I am very pleased to hear the assurance of the minister with regard to this matter. He said that if there was any demand an inquiry would be granted. I can only assure him of this: That the largest farmers' association in the West, consisting of the Saskatchewan grain growers, that assembled1 in convention last February'-representing between twenty-five and thirty thousand members-passed a resolution asking for an inquiry. I have also received a great many letters since I have been in Ottawa here from local associations urging me to ask for an inquiry, but they all agree that they do not want an inquiry by a commission composed of the same personnel as was the commission appointed by the late government.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: There is no use wasting time about that.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: The minister says there is no use wasting time about it. 1 am very glad indeed to hear his statement. The minister made the remark that there had been many investigations into the grain trade. So there has; but I would point out that there is nothing in the world, within my knowledge, which is quite so easy to manipulate and mix as wheat. There is nothing that lends itself so readily to manipulation; and my experience has been that there is a new trick played every year, Just as fast as we get on to the old trick they adopt a new one the following year.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I shall have to go West and learn some of the tricks.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
Yes, sir, go as far as Fort William and Port Arthur, and you will learn lots of them. It is pretty hard to quarrel with my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) when he adopts that benevolent go-to-Sunday-meeting-tonal, but I have got to disagree with him just a little bit. I have here a sample of the literature which was strewn all over our country at election time. Every day three or four epistles of the kind would arrive at my house. They were addressed to my sons, not to me. I must have been on the black list, but of course, the boys used
1 a.m. to hand them to me, and wherever I went through the campaign I encountered bushels of them.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I would like to see one.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: There were bushels of them and every one contained some reference to "Voting for Meighen."

What I meant was
that anything that deals with any enquiries made by the Grain Enquiry Commission is relevant to this item and may be discussed; but there was a reason, as I stated, for the hon. member for Marquette being given an opportunity to make a statement regarding something which had happened which more or less reflected upon him and some of his business associates.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
I am going to point out something which, I think, should be investigated. There was also a charge during the last campaign, but that is only in-

Grain Commission
cidental, and that is the selling of farmers' grain without permission. It was stated that there would not be any more of this if we elected our friends to the right. There never should have been any of it, if the commission had done its duty. The Grain Commission in the past has absolutely failed to do its duty in this respect. Let me point out how this works out. When a farmer sends his grain down to the head of the lakes and it is ordered to be held, he is paying storage on that grain until he sells it. When he has forwarded it, he has probably borrowed $1,000 on a car expecting that that grain will be held in the terminal elevator until he orders it to be sold. Immense quantities of grain have been sold without the farmer's permission, and he has been charged storage that he has not occupied. He has been charged interest on his money when his grain has been sold contrary to his orders and the firms have been using his money. His very object of withholding his grain from the market has been defeated because his grain has been sold contrary to his orders. That is a thing which would be a proper scope for an investigation. It has been proved over and over again. The attitude of our commission men who allow mills, contrary to the farmer's orders to draw grain which is passing those mills, is another matter which should be investigated. When wheat passes through Moosejaw, Kenora, through any of those places where those mills are grinding wheat, large quantities of it are stopped there without the farmer's permission or knowledge, and even cars which have been ordered to be sold are stopped and unloaded there without his permission. It is all this kind of thing which adds to the farmer's-I was going to say-contempt, for a commission which does not work as it ought to do. If the enquiry which is to be carried on, will have in view only one object, namely, the bettering of conditions in the grain trade, it will be welcomed by honest dealers. I am not here to assert that every man engaged in the grain business is a crook by any means. There are as many honest men in that trade as are to be found anywhere else; but there are a few others.
As regards my own company, my leader (Mr. Crerar) said that this investigation will be welcomed by the Farmers' companies. When the last commission was appointed we had no faith in either Mr. Staples, or Mr. Haslam who, in our western country, is considered a joke as regards the grain trade. Mr. Haslam is a man with a great deal of knowledge, but he does not seem to be able to apply it. When, however, we knew that that commission was appointed, our board passed a resolution instructing our officials to give the commission access to our books, documents, to give them all the information they had and all the assistance they possibly could. That was the attitude of the Saskatchewan Co-operative Elevator company. We felt that we had nothing to fear from any investigation into the grain trade, and now that the minister has assured us that the personnel will be different, we shall welcome an investigation, and I am quite in favour of this amount or any other amount which is necessary in order that a thorough enquiry may be had.

speechtext: We should have some explanation from the minister as to the scope of this work, as to whether or not it is proposed to extend it in any particular, and the possibilities of the future as regards this particular work. It is a matter of the utmost importance and we should know something about it.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
I think the request of my
hon. friend is quite reasonable; but I am quite sure neither of us desires to remain here too long. He will notice, as I am sure he has noticed from the commercial bulletin issued weekly, that the trade agents that we have in different parts of the world are advertising Canada and advising the department here, and that the department is spreading information throughout the country as to the requirements of different countries. In addition to the offices which we already have, it has been represented to us that there are possibilities of trade in Mexico, and the department looks favourably on that. We have a man in training now who understands that language, and it is proposed to send him to Mexico to look into the situation before we recommend a steamship subsidy which seems to be necessary to get much business. There are greater possibilities for the Mexican trade on the Pacific than on the Atlantic coast, because, as my hon. friends will understand, we do not, on the Pacific coast, come into such close competition with the southern States. The southern States have some advantage over Canada on the Atlantic coast; they are nearer to that country. Then it has been represented to
Trade and Commerce

us. that there might he possibilities of extending trade down into other parts of the southern Pacific Dominions, and we have been looking into that as well as into trade with Scandinavian countries.
My hon. friends will observe that there are some increases in the estimated amount required. That is to provide for the additional services which may develop and also to provide for a little more money for our trade missionaries who are out in foreign countries, so that they can better represent Canada. It has been represented to us by Canadians returning from these different countries that Canada heretofore has been a little niggardly with its trade agents outside in the way of providing accommodation. Sometimes they are doing business on a back street when they should be in a more business part of the city. The additional estimates are to give the department an opportunity of helping them to spread out somewhat more and represent Canada as we wish to be represented, as a first class country. I hope hon. gentlemen will allow this to go through. We have had almost a month's debate on trade conditions, and while I do not desire to refuse anything, I see no good purpose to be served by attempting at this early hour in the morning to make a speech on trade conditions throughout the country.

subtopic: TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I hope the Government will take this matter up and deal with it in a big way. The holding of a proper Canadian national exhibition in France would do a great deal to stimulate our trade with that country, and trade should always follow the flag and we should trade with France and our devoted Allies in the Great War and not with Germany. In view of our relations with France in the late war we should seek to develop as extensive a trade as possible with her. A French train was exhibited through Canada last summer, visiting the Canadian National Exhibition and many of the fall fairs. The government of France have for some time been considering erecting a trade building in connection with the Canadian National Exhibition. The French train that went through Canada excited much interest on the part of business men and was a demonstration of what could be done by the Government of Canada towards securing a proper exhibition in France. I hope that the Government will do everything possible to promote further trade with that country.

I do not see why we
should have any special Canadian representation in the United States. As far as I can see we have sufficient representation there now. Our representation through the British Ambassador at Washington is one of the few remaining things that bind Canada to the Mother Country. I am opposed to this vote, and I believe the people of the country will take the same view as I do. I do not think there is any special demand for a Canadian representative at Washington. I do not see what he could have to do that could not be done by the British Ambassador.
